posts.title: A new meta analysis says the effect is much bigger, and why I am not using it
posts.body:
A new study landed that would make my argument easier to sell.

I am not going to use it that way.

The paper is a peer reviewed meta analysis of social media use and adolescent mental health. It reports a pooled correlation of r = 0.308.

If you already believe social media is harming children that might sound like the confirmation you have been waiting for, and I build something for parents who are worried about exactly this, so a number like that would suit me.

Which is why I read past it.

The analysis pools 12 studies contributing 15 effect sizes, and it reports heterogeneity of I squared = 93.85 percent. Put plainly, the studies inside it disagree with each other so much that averaging them tells you very little about any one of them, and nothing about your own child.

Two more things.

A correlation is not proof that social media caused anything. And one pooled measure of social media use cannot tell us what a particular child watched, who they spoke to, what happened at bedtime, or what else was going on in their life.

The authors also report differences across school stages. That is worth investigating. It is not a sound basis for calling younger children the most vulnerable.

The summary does not say which countries the studies come from, so I would not carry any of it across to children here.

None of that makes the paper wrong. It deserves to be read and set beside the other evidence. But a result that points the way I would like deserves the same scrutiny as one that does not. Probably more.

It is the reason the stage check we built asks three questions about one child, yours, and promises nothing about what happens next.

The paper is linked in the comments.

If this is how you want evidence handled, repost it. The response should be in proportion to the evidence, and that has to cut both ways.

When did you last turn down a number that suited you?
posts.comment:
The paper: https://doi.org/10.1177/13591045261487468

The strongest objection is that a peer reviewed meta analysis is still useful evidence even when its studies differ. Agreed. I am not rejecting the paper or the correlation it reports. My caution is about treating a pool of correlational studies that disagree this much as a settled answer about any one child.
posts.checked: From the Research Radar, research GDC-RR-0754a1641c. ChatGPT wrote v1 from the reviewed handoff; this is my edit of it, v2. 27 of 27 automatic checks passed, including every figure against the five the review cleared. I am both the editor and the reviewer of v2, so whether it sounds like you is yours to judge. Text only, no card has been made. Not approved until you say so.
posts.hook: A new study landed that would make my argument easier to sell.
posts.share: A new meta analysis reports a much bigger link between social media and teenage mental health than the studies I usually quote. It would suit my argument, which is why I read past the headline number. The studies inside it disagree with each other so much that the average tells you very little.

ideas.t: The trial that lands after the law does
ideas.s: A Cambridge led UK trial, the IRL trial, randomly assigns students to one hour a day on TikTok and Instagram. It starts this month. Results are expected summer 2027.
ideas.a: The ban is reported to start March 2027. The first proper test of the thing it is banning reports months later. We are legislating first and testing second, and that is the whole Wrong Villain argument in one timeline.
ideas.p: Our thesis that a delay is not preparation, and the stage check.

ideas.t: The thing already in the toy box
ideas.s: A BSI survey of 1,000 UK parents in May 2026 reported half of children already have an AI enabled toy and 38 percent own two or more. Common Sense Media found 27 percent of AI toy outputs inappropriate for children and advises against them under five. Reporting says these toys sit outside the Online Safety Act.
ideas.a: Every hour of parliamentary time is going on social media while the unregulated thing is already in the house, bought by us, for Christmas.
ideas.p: Children and AI is our newest lane and the AI toy post did 3,173 in three weeks.

ideas.a: Not a post. A fact to check and correct in docs/11 and anywhere else we say spring.

news.title: Nobody gets a free pass
subjects: Nobody gets a free pass
Meta had a plan for its loudest critic
Are we judging the evidence, or whose side people are on?
news.subtitle: A court filing, a newspaper implication, and the week the argument stopped being about children.
news.body:
Court filings unsealed at the end of October show Meta employees discussing a whisper strategy against Jonathan Haidt.

Nobody has shown it was ever carried out.

Both of those sentences are true, and the gap between them is where I want to spend the next ten minutes, because that gap is the whole problem with how we argue about children and screens now.

What the filings show

The notes come from an internal meeting in March 2023, in a document headed Well-being Meeting Sound-check Notes. They talk about turning academics against Haidt, about getting the academic community to disavow him, and about finding someone to write a piece attacking his work. They were unsealed in the federal social media litigation in California, in front of Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, and reported from 27 October.

They are also a mess. Full of typos and shorthand, the kind of thing somebody types fast in a meeting where six people are talking. Reporters who have read them describe a brainstorm rather than a plan, and Meta has not commented.

I want to be careful about one line in particular. Two outlets reporting the same note give it differently, one as "turn academics against Haidt" and one with an extra word and a longer tail. I have not read the filing myself, because the court's document service refuses the tools I use, so I have described that line rather than put it in quotation marks. The phrase I am willing to quote is whisper strategy, because every outlet quotes it identically.

That may look like excessive care about two words. It is the entire point of this issue, so bear with me.

Then the story turned

Candice Odgers is one of the researchers who has challenged Haidt's conclusions. Her review of The Anxious Generation ran in Nature. She is Chancellor's Professor of Psychology and Informatics at the University of California, Irvine, and by her own count she has spent twenty five years on child and adolescent mental health.

On 29 October she wrote that The Times had suggested she and other critics were paid by Meta.

Her answer was flat. Meta does not fund her research. She has never been approached by Meta to shape what she says publicly.

And her name is not in those Meta documents. Not once.

The link between the filing and the people who disagree with Haidt was made by readers, not by the filing.

So in the space of about three days we got a genuine disclosure about a company's media strategy, and then an insinuation that the company's critics were bought, and the second thing travelled on the back of the first.

Why this bothers me more than it should

The reasoning runs backwards, and once you see the shape of it you see it everywhere.

It goes like this. Her findings are inconvenient. Therefore her motives must be suspect. Therefore the findings can be set aside without ever being read.

That is not an argument. It is a way of avoiding one. And it works in every direction: you can run exactly the same move on Haidt, and plenty of people do, pointing at his book sales and his speaking fees as though a man who earns money from a position cannot also hold it sincerely.

I have had a very small taste of this myself. Question the size of an effect in public and somebody will decide you are defending Big Tech.

I am not.

I want harmful design challenged, and I want researchers free to challenge a popular claim. Both of those things, at the same time, which is apparently an eccentric position to hold.

What the evidence actually says, which is the bit nobody is fighting about

What makes the motive fight so strange is that the underlying evidence isn't actually a mystery. It's just unsatisfying.

The US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine ran a consensus committee on this and published in December 2023. Its words, not mine:

> Available research that links social media to health shows small effects and weak associations, which may be influenced by a combination of good and bad experiences. Contrary to the current cultural narrative that social media is universally harmful to adolescents, the reality is more complicated.

And on the question everyone actually wants answered, whether social media causes the decline:

> The committee's review of published literature did not support the conclusion that social media causes changes in adolescent health at the population level.

I have read that document rather than a summary of it, because I have been caught out before by a number that turned out to be somebody's paraphrase of somebody's press release.

Now the part that cuts against me as much as anyone. The same report says the rigorous study designs that would settle the causal question are severely lacking. That is not a win for my side. It means my confidence should be lower too, and I am saying so in writing so that you can hold me to it.

Small average effects. Weak associations. Not enough good evidence to settle causation. That's the honest state of the field, and it's nobody's banner.

What Haidt is right about, which I should say more often

I've spent three sections being careful about his critics, so let me be careful about him too.

The thing Jonathan Haidt is right about is that parents aren't imagining the problem. Something changed in the lives of adolescents over roughly the period he describes, parents noticed it before researchers did, and the instinct to dismiss parental observation as moral panic has been wrong before and is a bad habit dressed up as rigour.

He's also right that the burden of proof has been placed in a strange spot. We generally don't ask parents to wait for randomised evidence before worrying about something their child does for four hours a day. Nobody demanded effect sizes before we put seatbelts in cars.

Where I part company is the size of the effect and the confidence of the conclusion. A generation rewired is a claim about mechanism and magnitude, and the mechanism and magnitude are the two things the evidence is weakest on. The National Academies committee, which had no book to sell, looked at the same literature and could not get there.

Both of those can be true. He can be right that something is wrong and wrong about how much of it is the phones. That combination is unsatisfying and it's where I actually live.

The one thing the Academies did recommend

Something gets lost when a report is reduced to "the effects are small", and it's the part nobody quotes.

The same committee that refused to conclude social media causes population level harm also proposed a set of practical steps, including design transparency at the platform level, broader education for young people and training for the adults around them, and action to reduce online harassment.

Read that list again. Not one of those is a ban, and not one of them is nothing.

That's the shape of the position that no camp is recruiting for: the evidence doesn't support the loudest claim, and the absence of a loud claim doesn't mean there's nothing to do.

Which is exactly why we fight about motives instead

A careful answer does not move anybody. "The effects look small and the designs are weak" has never once been shouted at a select committee.

So both camps reach for something that does move people. One side reaches for alarm, because a generation rewired is a story and an epidemic has a start date. The other side has started reaching for conspiracy, because a company plotting against a critic is also a story.

And the second one is newer, which is why I am writing about it. The people whose job is correcting overreach have started overreaching. A Psychology Today piece last month cited a BMJ paper as proof that Australia's ban had failed. The paper does not say the ban failed. It says we cannot tell yet, and its own authors say the full picture may take a decade.

When the referees start playing, a parent has nobody left to read.

What a parent is supposed to do with a field like this

I think there's an unspoken assumption in most writing about children and screens, which is that the reader will eventually be told what the answer is.

They won't be. Not this decade.

So the useful question isn't what the evidence says, it's how to act while the evidence is unsettled, and those are different skills. The second one nobody teaches.

What I've landed on is that the size of your response should match the confidence of the evidence, and the confidence here is low. Low confidence doesn't mean do nothing. It means prefer the actions that are cheap if you turn out to be wrong.

Talking to your child about why a feed shows them something is cheap if the effect of social media turns out to be tiny. Removing a phone for two years is expensive if it turns out to be tiny, because you've spent trust and taught nothing. That asymmetry is the whole of my position and it survives either outcome, which is the only reason I'm willing to hold it in public.

What this leaves you with on a Tuesday night

Nothing in the last two thousand words helps you with a thirteen year old who will not come off a screen. I know that. It is the uncomfortable fact underneath every piece of commentary on this subject, mine included.

So here is the one thing I would take from it, and it is a reading habit rather than a parenting tip.

When you next see a study about children and screens in your feed, ask what the finding would look like if it were small. Not whether the study is right or wrong, and certainly not who funded it. Just: if the true effect here were modest, what would the headline look like? Almost always, the answer is that it would look exactly like the headline you are reading, because a modest finding and a dramatic one are written up the same way.

That one question does more for you than knowing whose side anybody is on.

What to do on Sunday

Pick one claim about screens that you currently believe and that would change what you do if it turned out to be wrong. Write it on the back of an envelope. Then write what would have to be true for you to drop it.

That is it. Not a quiz for your child, a sentence for yourself. I have done it twice this year and dropped something both times, and the second one stung.

If you want somewhere to start with the child rather than the argument, our stage check asks three questions about your own child and gives you a stage with the things worth practising next. I will say plainly what it is: a starting point, not a measurement. We have no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards, and almost nobody in this field does.

Meta's motives deserve scrutiny. So does Haidt's evidence. So does Candice Odgers' evidence.

Nobody gets a free pass, and that has to include me.

news.title: The age is the easy part
subjects: The age is the easy part
Thirteen, sixteen, eighteen: three answers about the same child
I built a product around the word readiness and I cannot test it
news.subtitle: Three different legal ages for one child in one year, and not one of them came from evidence about children.
news.body:
I have built a product around the word readiness and I still cannot tell you how to test it.

That is the uncomfortable centre of this, and picking a better age does not make it go away.

Three answers about the same child, in the same year

Consider one child, turning thirteen this year in Britain.

She can open an account on most platforms, because thirteen is the minimum in most terms of service. She cannot use social media once the new restriction starts, because that line is drawn at sixteen. And she cannot have an open ended conversation with an AI companion on Character.AI, because that company closed those to under eighteens from 25 November 2025.

Thirteen, sixteen, eighteen.

Same child, same year, three different answers about what she's ready for.

Everyone is arguing about which number is correct. Almost nobody is asking why there are three.

Where each number actually comes from

Thirteen is the oldest and the weakest. It is the platform minimum written into terms of service across the industry, and it traces back to American children's privacy law rather than to any finding about what thirteen year olds can do. It is a compliance threshold that became a developmental claim by repetition. Nobody studied thirteen year olds and concluded thirteen.

Sixteen is the UK restriction, announced in June 2026. The Culture Secretary has named March 2027 as the start, though the regulations that would fix that date had not been laid when I wrote this, and official statements have also said spring 2027. Sixteen is a political number, arrived at through a political process, and I do not mean that as an insult. Parliament has to pick something.

Eighteen is the newest and the most interesting, because a company picked it rather than a government. Character.AI ended open ended chats for under eighteens from 25 November 2025, after lawsuits and an inquiry from the US Federal Trade Commission, replacing them with something narrower and more creative. That was a legal risk calculation, not a developmental one.

So we have a compliance threshold, a political compromise and a liability decision. Three entirely different kinds of reasoning, and the only thing they have in common is that none of them started from the question of what a child at that age can actually do.

Why an age is so attractive anyway

I want to be fair to the people drawing these lines, because the alternative is harder than the critics admit.

An age is enforceable. It is auditable. It is the same for every child, so it cannot be applied unfairly to one and not another. A regulator can write it down, a company can implement it, and a court can rule on it. Those are real virtues and I would not want to design a system without something like them.

An age also protects a child whose parents are not paying attention, which is the argument I find hardest to answer. A readiness test that depends on an engaged adult does nothing for a child who does not have one.

So I am not against the number. I am against the pretence that the number is the hard part.

What an age cannot do

What an age cannot do is describe the child in front of you. I know this, having three very different children.

One child can turn thirteen without knowing that an AI which sounds caring does not care. Without understanding that a chatbot can be confidently wrong about something it has no business being confident about. Without noticing when a conversation is being kept going rather than finished. With no idea when to stop talking to a machine and go and find a person.

Another child can be eleven and spot all four.

The age tells you when the door opens.

It tells you nothing about who walks through it.

So what would a readiness test look like

Here is where I have to be honest about how little anyone has.

It is not a quiz. A child can pass a quiz on Monday and hand over their address on Friday, and I would rather have no test than one that gives a parent false confidence.

It is not a certificate either, because the whole point is that it moves. A child's readiness changes as they grow, and it changes again when the technology changes under them. Something that was true about a child in January can be false in September because an app added a feature.

And it cannot be a measurement of the child alone, which took me a long time to accept.

The closest I have got is three things a parent can see for themselves.

One. Can the child explain, in their own words, why this thing is showing them this? Not a definition of an algorithm. Their own account of why this video and not another. A nine year old can often do this better than an adult, and a thirteen year old who cannot is telling you something.

Two. Can they tell you about a time they stopped? Any time. Put the phone down, closed the app, left a group chat, decided not to send something. One real example from their own life. Not a promise about the future, a memory from the past.

Three. Do they come to you when something turns? And this one is not about the child at all.

Whether a child brings you a problem depends almost entirely on whether bringing you the last one went well enough that they would do it again. If the last time ended in a confiscated phone and a row, you have taught them to handle the next one alone. That is the real test, and the person being tested is the parent.

I find the third one uncomfortable to write because I've failed it. Years ago my son wouldn't come off a dance video and I threatened to take away Saturday football. I knew inside a minute I'd got it wrong, and what stayed with me wasn't the row. It was that I had nothing to give him instead.

What that looks like at different ages

The three signals don't change with age. What a good answer sounds like does, and I think this is where most readiness advice falls down, because it gives parents one standard for a nine year old and a fifteen year old.

At nine, on the first signal, you're listening for anything causal at all. "Because I watched one like it" is a complete pass at nine. The child has noticed that their own behaviour and the screen's behaviour are connected, which is the whole foundation. On stopping, you want one example of leaving a game when something felt off, even if the reason was boring. On telling you, this is the age where it's almost entirely about you: a nine year old who has been shouted at once will go quiet for a year.

At twelve, the answers should get more specific and usually get worse, because this is the age where a child starts managing you. On the first signal you want more than cause and effect. You want them to notice that the thing showing them this wants something. On stopping, "I came off because I was bored" is not the same as "I came off because I noticed I'd been on it for an hour and I didn't like it". On telling you, twelve is where most families lose the thread, and it's almost always because the previous report was met with a consequence rather than a conversation.

At fifteen, the honest version is that you're no longer testing them, you're asking them. A fifteen year old can usually explain a recommender system better than their parents. What they often can't do is apply it to themselves in the moment, which is a developmental fact rather than a character flaw. On telling you, at fifteen the useful question isn't whether they'd come to you, it's who they would go to, and the right answer doesn't have to be you.

None of that is validated. It's what I've got from asking, and I'd rather give you something specific enough to be wrong than something vague enough to be safe.

The objection I find hardest

There's one argument against all of this that I haven't been able to answer, and it would be dishonest to leave it out.

A readiness approach depends on an adult who's paying attention. An age doesn't.

If the question is what protects the child whose parents are absent, exhausted, unwell or simply not interested, then a blunt age limit does something that a thoughtful conversation at the kitchen table cannot, because the conversation never happens. The children most likely to be harmed are the least likely to have the adult that my entire approach assumes.

I don't have a good response to that. The weak response, which is still true, is that a line at sixteen doesn't give that child an adult either; it gives them a slightly later start and the same lack of help. The better response is that this is exactly why the drivers nobody legislates about matter more than the platform does, and that's a different newsletter.

But I'm not going to pretend the objection doesn't land. It does.

Where that leaves our own product, stated plainly

Our stage check is an attempt at this, and I will not dress it up as more.

Three questions about your own child, and a stage with the things worth practising next. A starting point rather than a measurement.

We have no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards, and almost nobody in this field does. If anyone knows of a readiness instrument for children online that has been tested against what children actually do later, I would genuinely like to read it, and I will say so in this newsletter if it changes my mind.

That admission costs me something to publish. It is also the reason I think this is worth reading rather than the reason it is not.

The part the ban cannot reach

In March, or in spring, a line will be drawn at sixteen. Whatever you think of it, something will change on that day and something will not.

What changes is access. What does not change is whether a fifteen year old understands why the rule exists, what they do with a friend's login, and whether they come and tell you when something lands in their feed that they did not choose.

A deadline is not a plan. It is not nothing either, and I have stopped pretending otherwise. It buys time. The question nobody is answering is what the time is for.

What to do on Sunday

Ask your child the second question, because it is the easiest one and the one most likely to get a real answer.

"Tell me about a time you stopped."

Not tonight, if tonight is already difficult. On a Sunday, in the car or doing something else, when nobody is being examined. Then say nothing and let them think.

If they have an example, you have learned something worth more than any age. If they do not, you have also learned something, and now you know what to practise.

An age tells you when the door opens. This tells you who is walking through it.

news.title: What you would have to hand over
subjects: What you would have to hand over
A passport, a bank check, or your child's face
The ban needs a way to know who is sixteen
news.subtitle: Ofcom has named four ways to prove a child is sixteen. Each one fixes a problem and asks your family for something else.
news.body:
A ban on social media for under sixteens needs a way to know who is sixteen.

That sentence sounds obvious and it is the most consequential thing about the whole policy, because the method is where the ban actually touches your house.

On 29 October Ofcom published a rapid assessment of highly effective age assurance at sixteen. It names four ways of doing it. Nobody has asked parents what they think of any of them, so this issue is my attempt at the plain English version, written before the consultation rather than after it.

The four

Ofcom's four are photo ID matching, digital ID services, banking based checks, and facial age estimation. Its own phrase for them is methods currently capable of being highly effective, and the word currently is doing real work in that sentence.

Take each in turn, and in each case ask the only question that matters to a family: what are you handing over?

Photo ID matching. Your child uploads a passport or a driving licence and a selfie, and software checks they match. You are handing over a government identity document and a biometric image of a child's face, usually to a third party vendor rather than to the platform itself. The upside is accuracy. The downside is that you have created a record linking a named child to an account.

Digital ID services. Your child proves their age once, with a provider, and then reuses that proof across services. You hand over the same documents as above, but only once, which is genuinely better. What you get in exchange is a persistent identity that sits behind every app your child uses, and a single company that knows a great deal about where a child goes.

Banking based checks. The platform asks a bank to confirm, yes or no, that this person is over sixteen. You hand over a connection between a child's bank and a social media account. The attraction is that the bank already knows and does not have to say anything else. The discomfort is the precedent of a financial institution acting as the gatekeeper for speech.

Facial age estimation. Your child looks at a camera and software estimates their age from the image. You hand over a scan of a child's face. No document, which is the appeal, and the images are generally not retained, which is the mitigation. But it is an estimate, and that matters more at sixteen than anywhere else.

The accuracy problem at exactly the wrong age

Facial age estimation gets more accurate the further you are from the line. It is very good at telling a forty year old from a twelve year old. It is at its weakest around the age the ban is drawn at.

Ofcom's response is a challenge age. If a scan puts someone close to sixteen, the service should check them a second way rather than guess. That is sensible and I have no complaint about it.

I do want to flag one thing I have seen stated as fact and will not repeat. A compliance vendor's summary of Ofcom's assessment describes a margin of error of a few years at sixteen. I cannot find Ofcom stating the margin in years anywhere, and Ofcom's site refuses the tools I use, so I have not read the primary document. The remedy is confirmed. The size of the problem is not, and I would rather tell you that than round it up.

Who gets left out

This is the part I think is underdiscussed, because every conversation about age checks is about the children who get through and almost none is about the children who cannot get in.

An estimated 94 percent of people aged sixteen and over hold a passport or a driving licence. About 90 percent of sixteen and seventeen year olds hold a bank account. Those two figures sound reassuring until you turn them over: roughly one in ten of that age group has no bank account, and a slice has neither document.

The number doing the rounds for sixteen and seventeen year olds who hold neither a passport nor a licence is 150,000. I want to be precise about where that comes from, because I have seen it credited to Ofcom and it is not Ofcom's. It is an estimate from CitizenCard, drawn from a survey of 8,459 sixteen and seventeen year olds in schools, which Ofcom itself describes as a non representative sample. Treat it as an order of magnitude rather than a count.

Even as an order of magnitude it tells you something. A system built on documents will work smoothly for most families and badly for the ones who already find official systems hard: children in care, children in families without passports, children whose paperwork is somewhere else. Those are not the households with the most slack.

I notice that the privacy argument and the exclusion argument point in opposite directions, which is why this is genuinely hard. The method that asks for the least, a face scan, is the one that works for everybody. The method that is most accurate, a passport, is the one that excludes.

What happens to it afterwards

Every conversation about age checks stops at the moment of the check. The more important question is what happens to the thing you handed over in the weeks after.

In most of these designs the platform doesn't do the checking. A third party vendor does, and the number of companies holding children's identity documents goes up rather than down. Facial age estimation is the best placed here, because a well built implementation estimates and discards. Document checks are the worst, because a document has to be stored somewhere for at least as long as it takes to review an appeal.

That last word is where I'd look hardest. The checks themselves will mostly work. It's the appeals process that collects the documents, because a child wrongly estimated as under sixteen has to prove otherwise, and proving otherwise means uploading something.

We already have an example of what that looks like when it goes wrong. In October 2025 Discord said approximately 70,000 users may have had government ID photos exposed at a third party used to review age appeals. The attackers claimed a far higher figure and Discord called that an extortion bluff; no outside party has verified any of the numbers, and Discord has since moved to different providers. I'm not offering that as a prediction and I'm certainly not saying it will happen here.

I'm saying that the appeals queue is where the documents pile up, and that no part of Ofcom's four methods is the part that gets written about.

Ask it as one question. Not "is this check accurate", but "who holds the file, for how long, and what happens when my child is told no?"

The fair case for all of it

I have been describing costs, so let me put the other side as well as I can, because the people who want this have a real answer.

Checks are the price of a rule that means anything. The alternative is the system we have now, which is a box a child ticks, and that system has produced a situation where a nine year old can be on a platform designed for adults by typing a different year. If you think the current arrangement is unacceptable, then something has to actually verify something, and every method of verifying involves handing something over.

A ban with real checks is a better ban than one without them. Ofcom's assessment is a serious piece of work by people trying to make a hard thing function, and the twelve month commitment to publish research on circumvention after the ban starts is the kind of thing regulators usually avoid promising.

I can hold both of those at once: that this is a serious attempt, and that nobody has asked a parent which trade they would accept.

What a check decides, and what it does not

Here is the line I keep coming back to.

A check decides who gets through the door.

It does not decide what a fifteen year old does with a friend's login. It does not decide what they feel when something odd lands in their feed at eleven at night. It does not decide whether they tell you.

Ofcom is honest about the first part of this. Its own assessment says no age assurance method is "completely robust against circumvention by children", and it expects attempts to increase once there is something to circumvent. That is the regulator saying out loud that the door will be got round.

So the door matters.

The door is not the plan.

And there's a second order effect worth naming, because it's the one I expect to be surprised by. Every one of these four methods makes a child's online life more identified than it is today. A teenager who currently moves through the internet as nobody in particular will, after March or whenever it lands, move through it as a verified person of a known age. That's the point, and it's also a change in what it means to be young online, made as a side effect of a child protection measure rather than as a decision anybody voted on.

I don't know whether that's bad. I know it's large, and that it isn't what the debate has been about.

The timeline, so you can see what is actually decided

As things stand: the restriction was announced in June 2026. Ofcom published its assessment on 29 October. The first regulations were due before the end of 2026 and had not been laid when I wrote this. The Culture Secretary has named March 2027, though no exact date is officially confirmed and official statements have also said spring 2027. Ofcom will consult on draft guidance once the regulations are laid, and will publish research on circumvention within twelve months of the ban taking effect.

Which means the method is not settled. There is a consultation coming on how this will actually work, and parents are not usually the loudest voice in those.

What to do on Sunday

Decide, before anyone asks you, which of the four you would accept for your own child. Not in the abstract. Actually pick one.

A passport upload. A reusable digital ID. A bank check. A face scan.

I find that choosing makes the whole argument different, because it stops being about whether the ban is good and becomes about what you are willing to trade. When the consultation opens, you will already have an answer, and an answer given early is worth more than an objection raised late.

And then the other half, which is the half I build for. Whatever method you would accept, it will not tell your child anything. The understanding has to come from somewhere else, and the time between now and March is the only part of this that is yours.

If you want a starting point, our stage check asks three questions about your own child and gives you a stage with the things worth practising next. A starting point, not a measurement: we hold no outcome evidence that finishing a stage changes what a child does.

news.title: The syllabus a law wrote
subjects: The syllabus a law wrote
A ban is already teaching. The question is what.
Half of them said nobody ever checked
news.subtitle: Australia banned social media for under sixteens. Three months in, the clearest result is a lesson nobody intended to teach.
news.body:
Nobody can tell you yet whether banning under sixteens from social media works.

Australia can already tell you what it teaches.

The numbers, three months in

Australia's online safety regulator went back three months after its ban began and surveyed 803 children aged ten to fifteen. Before the ban, nearly 86 percent were using at least one age restricted platform. After, still above 81 percent.

A separate study from the University of Newcastle, published in the BMJ, recruited 436 adolescents and followed up with 408 of them. It found insufficient evidence that use had meaningfully fallen.

One thing did move, and almost nobody quotes it. The share of children who actually held an account fell from 52.4 percent to 42.1 percent. The regulator calls that modest and statistically significant. It is the one measurable thing the ban has done so far and it is missing from both sides of the argument, which tells you something about how the argument is conducted.

I am not going to tell you the ban failed. The regulator says plainly that its report is not an assessment of whether platforms complied, the BMJ paper's own authors say the full picture may take a decade, and it is one country with self reported answers. Anyone claiming three months settles this has not read it.

Then look at how

This is the part that stopped me.

The BMJ study found the routes you would expect. Fake accounts, someone else's account, private browsing. VPN use was the smallest at two to three percent, which is worth saying because VPNs are what everyone assumes.

The regulator found something blunter. Of the children who still had accounts, about half said the platform had never checked their age. And 37 percent had simply put themselves down as sixteen or over.

Read that again.

Not circumvented. Not hacked. Typed a different number into a box.

That's the single most consequential finding in either study, and it arrived as a footnote in both. We spent two years arguing about whether a ban could be enforced, and the answer turns out to be that in roughly half of cases nobody attempted to enforce it at all.

The lesson, and who delivered it

That is a child's first real lesson in digital life, and a law delivered it.

The lesson is that identity online is something you assert, and nobody checks.

I do not think anybody intended to teach that. A law was passed to protect children and its most measurable early effect has been to demonstrate, at national scale, that the gate is a formality. Hundreds of thousands of children now have direct personal experience of saying they are older than they are and nothing happening.

And once a child knows that, they know it for everything. Not just social media. Every age gate, every terms of service, every box that asks for a date of birth.

We taught it first

Before I get too comfortable, the uncomfortable half.

Parents were always the teacher here. A survey of a thousand American parents, published in First Monday in 2011, found that around a third had a child who joined Facebook before turning thirteen, and that two thirds of those parents helped set the account up. The authors' point was not that those parents were careless. It was that an age rule parents do not accept gets opened by the parents.

I am in no position to be smug about it. During Covid we had two small girls at home and a business to keep alive, and we used YouTube as a babysitter to get through the day.

A ban only changes the syllabus. It does not change who is standing at the front.

None of which makes the ban wrong

I want to resist the pull of my own argument here, because it would be easy to turn all of the above into "so the ban is pointless" and that is not what I think.

A protected period is worth having. If a thirteen year old spends two more years not being recommended content by a system optimised for engagement, that is two years, and two years at that age is a long time.

A deadline is not a plan. It is not nothing either.

What it buys is time. What nobody is answering is what the time is for.

France looked at its own version and struck it down

There is a useful counterweight from a country that got further than most.

In August, France's constitutional council struck down the under fifteen ban at the heart of its own new law, two weeks before it was due to start. The rest of the law stands.

The main ground was proportionality: a blanket ban on every under fifteen, whatever the child and whatever the service, was out of proportion. The second ground was separate and in some ways more interesting. Parliament had written no legal safeguards for a scheme that, to work at all, requires every user to prove their age, adults included.

That is the age check problem arriving by the back door. You cannot check children without building a system that checks everybody, and France's highest constitutional authority decided that parliament had not thought about what that meant.

Britain has its own version coming, and the argument will be the same one.

What both sides are counting

Something I notice about every piece of commentary on the Australian experiment, including some of mine.

Both sides are counting the same thing. Whether children got in. Whether children were kept out.

Nobody is counting what a sixteen year old can actually do.

The eighteen percent nobody mentions

There's a third figure in the regulator's report that I think is the most interesting of the lot, and I've not seen anyone quote it.

Eighteen percent of the children who still had accounts said they'd been wrongly estimated as over sixteen.

Not that they lied. That the system looked at them and guessed wrong in their favour.

That's a different problem from the 37 percent who typed a false age, and it's a worse one, because it can't be fixed by better enforcement of honesty. It's the age estimation technology being asked to do something at the exact point where it's least reliable, which is around the threshold itself.

And it cuts both ways, which is the part that should worry a parent more than the circumvention. If the system wrongly waves through eighteen percent of under sixteens, it's also wrongly stopping some number of sixteen and seventeen year olds who are entitled to be there. Nobody surveys those children, because a child who's been refused doesn't show up in a study of children who got in.

So what should the protected period contain

If a ban buys two years, the obvious question is what goes in them, and I've not seen a government anywhere answer it.

Here's the test I'd apply to any proposal. Does it change what the child can reach, or does it change what the child can do? Almost everything on offer is the first kind. Age checks, device limits, school phone policies, app timers: all access, none judgement.

The second kind is harder to legislate because it can't be audited. You cannot inspect a school and confirm that a fourteen year old would notice a feed narrowing. There's no checkbox for it, which is exactly why it keeps losing to things that have checkboxes.

What I'd want in those two years is narrow and unglamorous. That a child can say why something is being shown to them. That they've stopped something once, on purpose, and can tell you about it. That when something turns, coming to an adult is a live option rather than a theoretical one.

Three things. None of them inspectable, all of them observable at your own kitchen table.

There is no measure, anywhere in any of this, of whether a young person leaving a protected period understands why a feed shows them what it shows them, or can notice when a conversation has quietly changed under them, or would tell an adult when something lands that they did not choose. We are measuring the door, in detail, repeatedly, and ignoring the room.

What Australia will actually be able to tell us, and when

Worth being clear about what this experiment can and can't deliver, because Britain is about to lean on it heavily in both directions.

Three months is nothing. The BMJ authors say the full picture may take a decade, and they're right for a boring reason: the children affected are still children. You cannot measure what a protected adolescence does to an adult until the adolescent is an adult.

What three months can show is implementation. Did the checks run. Did accounts close. Did children find routes round. All of that is answerable now, and all of it is about the machinery rather than the child.

What it cannot show is whether any of it helped.

So when somebody tells you Australia proves the ban works, or proves it failed, they're describing the machinery and calling it the outcome. The regulator itself says its report is not an assessment of whether platforms complied, which is a remarkably careful sentence for a regulator to publish about its own data.

My own prediction, recorded so you can hold me to it: the implementation numbers will keep improving, the circumvention numbers will keep falling, and in three years we still won't know whether Australian sixteen year olds are better off. Those are different questions and only one of them gets measured.

The thing I had nothing to say

Years ago my son was watching a dance video and would not come off it, and I threatened to take away Saturday football.

I knew inside a minute I had got it wrong. What stayed with me was not the row. It was that I had nothing to give him instead. I had a punishment and no alternative, which is the position a ban puts a whole country in.

We spent a lot of nine o'clocks after days like that wishing something existed that would help us manage the devices rather than just switch them off.

A ban switches them off. It does not sit down with your child.

What to do on Sunday

If a protected period is coming, the question is what happens during it, and that is not a government's job.

So: pick the one thing you would want your child to understand by the day the checks start, and name it out loud to them. Just one. Not a lecture and not a list.

Mine, for what it is worth, is that an account is a claim and not a fact. That everything online rests on somebody having said who they are, and that this applies to the person they are talking to as much as to them.

That single idea does more work than any number of hours saved, and it is the one thing the Australian data accidentally proved.

If you want the structured version, our stage check asks three questions about your own child and gives you a stage with the things worth practising next. A starting point rather than a measurement. We hold no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards, and I would rather say that than imply otherwise.

So if the door opens on your child's sixteenth birthday, what do you want them to come and tell you first?

news.title: Two governments, same mistake, opposite directions
subjects: Two governments, same mistake, opposite directions
Five years ago I would have shared that post
The trial is running. Nobody will say when it reports.
news.subtitle: Sweden threw out a policy for not being evidence based and replaced it with one that is not evidence based. Guess which got better press.
news.body:
Five years ago I would have shared the Sweden story without checking it.

Screens out of classrooms, printed textbooks back in. I thought screens were mostly bad for children and that school should stay close to paper and pen, so a country as digital as Sweden turning round would have gone straight onto my feed with something approving underneath it.

I changed my mind since, and not into the opposite camp, which is the part that takes longer.

The policy is real

Let me start with what is true, because the viral version is not invented, it is incomplete.

In 2023 Sweden threw out its own national digitisation plan. In 2024 it funded printed textbooks. From July 2025, under twos in preschool use analogue materials only.

All of that is accurate, and the reason given for scrapping the digitisation plan is the interesting bit: it was not sufficiently evidence based.

Hold that phrase.

What the viral version leaves out

Sweden's own education agency never called it a crisis.

Three Swedish researchers went back through how the 2021 international reading results were presented and found two different stories told about the same numbers. The National Agency for Education emphasised the positives. The government called it a reading crisis. Sweden had in fact moved up the league table and declined less than most countries did.

And the two of them named different culprits. The agency said the main problem in Swedish schooling was segregation. The government said digitalisation, migration, and not enough time spent reading.

Only one of those is a villain you can fix with a book order.

I want to sit on that for a moment, because it is the quiet centre of this whole newsletter. When a government picks a cause for a problem in children's outcomes, it is also picking what it will be asked to do about it. Segregation is expensive, slow and politically miserable. Screens are cheap, fast and nobody defends them.

Nobody has shown the books worked

There is no evaluation of the textbook policy. None.

International reading results published in September had Swedish reading down 21 points. I am not using that against the policy, and I want to be explicit about why: those students were born in 2009 and were schooled before the reform. It judges nothing. If I used it I would be doing exactly what I am criticising.

So we have a policy introduced to correct an insufficiently evidence based policy, with no evidence base of its own and no plan to build one.

The research is thinner than the story too

Paper does beat screen for reading. That part is real. Across 54 studies the advantage is about a fifth of a standard deviation.

Look only at children and it halves, with a confidence interval that still includes zero.

The handwriting brain study everyone quotes tested 36 university students. Not children. Thirty six undergraduates, and a 2025 commentary disputes the learning claim drawn from it.

I keep meeting the screens out of schools argument in its confident form, and the confident form is not what the literature supports. Nor, and this cuts the other way, does the literature support confident enthusiasm for classroom devices. Ferguson's 2025 paper on school smartphone bans is titled "remain unproven", and an English study of 1,227 students across 30 schools found no difference in wellbeing or attainment either way. I am not arguing for devices in classrooms. I am arguing that nobody has earned certainty.

Same move, opposite directions

So here is the shape of it. A government threw out one plan for not being evidence based, and replaced it with another that is not evidence based. Same move, opposite direction, and far better press for the second one.

That is not a Swedish failing. It is what happens when a problem is urgent, real, and politically legible, and the honest answer is "we do not know yet". Nobody gets re elected on "we do not know yet".

Which brings me home.

Britain is doing its own version right now

Britain has a social media restriction for under sixteens coming. The Culture Secretary has named March 2027, though no exact date is officially confirmed and official statements have also said spring 2027, and the regulations that would fix it had not been laid when I wrote this.

Meanwhile, in Bradford, something is happening that almost nobody has heard of.

The IRL Trial launched in secondary schools in autumn 2026. It is co led by Professor Amy Orben at Cambridge and Dr Dan Lewer at Born in Bradford, funded by Wellcome with a £1.2 million award from April 2026, and supported by the NIHR Yorkshire and Humber ARC. Around 4,000 students across years 8, 9 and 10, aged twelve to fifteen, in ten Bradford secondary schools. Half of each year group is randomly assigned a daily cap and a night time block on social media. The other half carries on as normal. The main outcome is self reported anxiety, with sleep, bullying, body image, school life and time with friends and family alongside it.

This is, as far as I can tell, the first serious British attempt to answer by experiment the question the ban is about to answer by legislation.

And after going looking twice, there's one thing I couldn't establish: nobody has published when it reports.

Not the trial's own pages. Not the university announcements. Not the funder's project listing. I can tell you when it started and I cannot tell you when it will tell us anything, and I spent real time trying.

Why that is the finding rather than a gap

I had intended to write that Britain legislates before the trial reports. I cannot write that, because I do not know when the trial reports, and writing it would be exactly the sort of confident claim this issue is complaining about.

What I can say is narrower and I think worse.

The country is about to restrict social media for under sixteens. The only large British randomised test of restricting social media for under sixteens is running right now, in ten schools in Bradford, and no public source will tell a parent when its answer arrives.

Nearly everything the rest of us quote, me included, shows an association. The IRL Trial is built to show what changes when use actually goes down, which is a different and much more useful thing. It will not answer every question about every child in six weeks, and the fair objection is that families and regulators cannot sit still waiting for perfect evidence about risks we already know are there. Both true.

It can still trade some of our confidence for a measurement, which I'll take.

Why the primary outcome is the thing to watch

One detail about the trial deserves more attention than it's had, because it determines what we'll be allowed to conclude.

The main outcome is self reported anxiety. Not sleep, not grades, not screen time. Anxiety, as reported by the young person.

That's a defensible choice and it's also the choice most likely to produce a result nobody is happy with. Self report is noisy. Six weeks is short for a mood measure. And teenagers who know they've been put in the limited group may answer differently for reasons that have nothing to do with their social media use, which is a problem every behavioural trial has and none of them solves.

So the honest expectation is a small effect with wide uncertainty, arriving into a public argument that has no vocabulary for small effects with wide uncertainty.

I'd rather say that in advance than after. If the trial finds nothing, that won't mean limits do nothing. If it finds something, it won't mean the ban is vindicated. It'll mean that in ten Bradford schools, over six weeks, a cap and a curfew moved a self reported number by some amount, and the interesting work will be in the secondary outcomes underneath.

Did they sleep more. Did bullying move. Did they spend the time with people, or move to a different screen.

That last one is the question I'd most like answered and the one least likely to make a headline.

The political economy of not knowing

I keep coming back to why "we don't know yet" is so hard to say from a podium, because once you see the incentive you see the same pattern in both countries.

A minister who says the evidence is thin owns the problem and gets no credit. A minister who names a cause and acts gets a headline and a policy, and the evaluation lands long after they've moved department. Sweden's digitisation plan was scrapped by people who will not be in post when the textbook policy is assessed, if it ever is.

None of that requires bad faith. It's just what the job rewards.

The only thing that breaks the cycle is somebody measuring afterwards, which is unglamorous, slow, and the first thing cut. Which is why a trial in ten Bradford schools with no publication date is a more important piece of public policy than most of what will be said about this in Parliament.

The part no researcher can hand you

A limit changes access. It does not teach judgement.

If a child gets six quieter weeks, something has to happen in the quiet, or they come out of it with the same instincts and a worse temper. That is as true of a six week trial as it is of a national ban, and it is the part that sits with a parent either way.

The fight in my house was never about which book my son was reading. It was about the thing in his hand that kept asking for him back. No book order reaches that, and no policy reaches it either.

A school can change its tools. A parent cannot.

So my bet, and I'll call it a bet rather than a finding, is on teaching a child to notice it.

That bet could lose. If the IRL Trial comes back showing that simply reducing access moves anxiety on its own, with no teaching attached, then I've been building the harder version of something a timer does for free, and I'll say so in this newsletter.

What to do on Sunday

When the next policy story about children and screens crosses your feed, from any direction, ask one question before you share it: has anyone evaluated this?

Not whether it sounds right. Not whether the country doing it seems sensible. Just whether a single soul has gone back afterwards and measured what happened.

For Sweden's textbooks, the answer is no. For the UK ban, the answer is not yet, and the one British study that might tell us is running in Bradford without a published reporting date.

That question would have stopped me sharing the Sweden post five years ago, and it is the only reading habit I have picked up since that I would recommend to anybody.

If you want the part that is yours rather than Westminster's, our stage check asks three questions about your own child and gives you a stage with the things worth practising next. A starting point, not a measurement: we hold no outcome evidence that finishing a stage changes what a child does.

news.title: A year of posting, and the thirteen clicks
subjects: A year of posting, and thirteen clicks
275,018 impressions and the number that embarrassed me
The same story, two openings, fourteen times the reach
news.subtitle: A year of LinkedIn, honestly audited, including the bit where I had been doing one thing wrong the whole time.
news.body:
In the last 365 days my LinkedIn posts were shown 275,018 times, up about 2,065 percent on the year before, and reached 114,314 people.

Thirteen of them clicked a link in a post.

Thirteen. For the year. Not thirteen percent, thirteen human beings.

The number that changed what I do

Over the same period, 165 people clicked the button on my profile.

So the profile outperformed every link in every post by more than twelve to one, and I had spent a year putting links in posts.

I knew in theory that LinkedIn suppresses posts with external links. Everybody who writes about this platform says so, usually with a confident percentage attached. What I did not have was my own number, and my own number is not a 25 to 60 percent penalty. It is thirteen clicks against 165, which is not a penalty so much as a different mechanism entirely.

The link is not a weak call to action. The link is not the call to action at all. The post is, and the profile is what collects.

The near controlled experiment I did by accident

This is the part I would not have believed if it had happened to somebody else.

I wrote about Australia's under sixteen ban twice, a couple of months apart. Same story, same evidence, same argument. Different opening.

The first version opened like this:

> Australia did the thing everyone is asking for. It banned social media for under sixteens. Eight in ten of those...

It did under 1,154 impressions. I cannot be more precise than that, because below a certain level the export stops giving exact figures, which is its own kind of verdict.

The second version opened like this:

> Australia banned social media for under 16s. Three months later, more than eight in ten of those teenagers were still on it.

It did 15,186.

Same subject. Same facts. Roughly fourteen times the reach.

What actually differs between those two openings

I have stared at this pair for a while, because if you can see the difference you can repeat it, and if you cannot you are just lucky.

The first one sets up. "Australia did the thing everyone is asking for" is a frame, and a frame asks the reader to wait. Then the fact arrives in the third sentence, by which point the reader has made a decision.

The second one is a complete sentence containing a number that contradicts what you expect. Banned, and then still on it. The contradiction is finished inside the first two lines, and the reader has been given something rather than promised something.

It is not that the second is shorter. It is that the second one closes a loop and the first one opens one.

Scanning the whole year against that test, the pattern holds up. Every one of my scene led openings, the ones that start with a moment in my own house, sits in the bottom third: 1,701, 1,167, 1,164. I like those posts. Some of them are the best writing I have done for the platform. They do not travel.

And the all time best, at 75,842, opens on a peer reviewed meta analysis of 46 studies and lands on a single strange number. Not a story. A number in a sentence that contradicts what the reader believes.

The thing I got wrong for a year

Here is the uncomfortable conclusion, and the reason I am writing this publicly rather than quietly adjusting.

I had a theory that opening with a personal scene builds trust, and trust is what this subject needs. It is a reasonable theory. I believed it for a year. My own data says it costs me roughly 90 percent of my reach.

The scenes are not wasted. They work in paragraph nine. They do not work in line one, and the difference between those two positions is a factor of ten.

I only found that out because I exported a year of data and read it against a rule instead of against my preferences.

What I still cannot tell you, which is the honest half

If this were a marketing newsletter it would stop at the lesson. Here is the part that makes me uneasy.

I do not know which image type works. The export records impressions, reactions, comments, engagement rate, post age and the opening line. It has no column for format. Every piece of format information I hold on a year of posting is four posts: one research card, which happens to be the 75,842, two posts carrying an article link, at 6,940 and 3,561 with engagement rates under half the text posts around them, and one native video at 1,164.

One card, one video and two link posts. That is not a finding, it is an anecdote with a spreadsheet. My own rule is that anything built on fewer than ten posts is a hypothesis, so the honest answer to "which image works" is that I have no idea and neither does anybody else looking at this account.

I do not know which newsletter issue ever worked. Twenty seven have gone out. I hold no open rate and no subscriber trend for any of them. Which means every editorial decision I have made about this newsletter for a year has been taste.

Both of those are one column in a spreadsheet away from being answerable, and I had not added the column, which is the same failure as the thirteen clicks: I was running on folklore where I could have been running on my own data.

The comments told a different story from the impressions

If I'd only sorted by reach I'd have drawn the wrong conclusion, so here's the correction my own data forced on me.

Across the year: 4,750 reactions and 1,712 comments. But the posts with the most comments weren't the posts with the most impressions, and they weren't close.

The 15,186 post, my second best for reach, ran at 0.73 percent engagement. Several posts that reached a tenth of that ran above 3 percent, and one hit 4.87 percent on 3,288 impressions.

So the surprising number recruits strangers. It does not start a conversation.

What starts a conversation is a named argument or a real question, and those posts reach fewer people and get answered properly. Two completely different jobs, and I'd been judging every post against one scoreboard.

That's changed how I plan a week. Not five posts all trying to go wide, but a reach post, an argument post, and an authority post, each judged against what it was for. The reach post goes first, because it raises the baseline the argument post lands into.

I'd have missed that entirely if I'd stopped at impressions, which is the real argument for exporting rather than eyeballing.

Seventy percent out of network, and why it's the only number that matters

Thirty percent of the reach came from people connected to me. Seventy percent came from strangers.

I'd been watching the wrong figure for a year. Total impressions goes up when your network grows, which means it partly measures how long you've been doing this rather than whether the writing works. The out of network share measures whether the platform is choosing to show your post to people who've never heard of you, and that's the only mechanism by which a small account becomes a bigger one.

Seventy percent is high. I didn't earn it by posting more.

I earned it, as far as I can tell, by staying in one subject. Children, screens, evidence. Nothing else, for a year, even when something else was tempting and topical. The 2026 shift in how LinkedIn ranks rewards consistency within one defined area over raw volume, and an account that wanders reads to the system as an account with no subject.

The practical version: the discipline that felt like a constraint was the thing doing the work.

One more figure in the same spirit: 801 saves against 121 reposts, six and a half to one. People were filing these privately rather than endorsing them publicly, which makes sense for a subject where you're either the parent who's too relaxed or the parent who's too strict. A high save to repost ratio means your audience is being careful, not uninterested, and I'd been reading it as the second thing.

The three rules I would give anyone writing about a contested subject

Open on a number inside a complete sentence that contradicts what the reader expects. Not a bare number, not a number delayed to sentence three. The exception that also works is declared uncertainty, saying out loud what you cannot do: two of my best performers for the year were admissions rather than assertions. Neither beats the other, and both beat a scene.

Put nothing in the body that asks the reader to leave. The post earns the reader, the profile collects them. My ratio is thirteen to 165 and I suspect yours is similar.

Export your own numbers before you believe anyone's percentages, including mine. Every figure in this issue is from my own account. The agency blog numbers I had been carrying around turned out to be directionally right and quantitatively useless.

The one thing to do this week

Export your last year. Sort by impressions. Then read the first two lines of your top five and your bottom five next to each other, and say out loud what differs.

It took me twenty minutes and it changed how I write. You may find the opposite of what I found, in which case I'd genuinely like to hear it, because a single account is a sample of one and I've just spent a newsletter being careful about exactly that kind of claim.

Before I exported it I'd have told you with real confidence that scene led openings were my strongest work. My memory of my own performance wasn't slightly wrong. It was inverted.

Mine was thirteen. What's yours?
