I exported a year of my own LinkedIn numbers and one of them embarrassed me.

275,018 impressions. 114,314 people. Thirteen clicks on links in posts, for the whole year. The profile button got 165.

So I went through the rest of it properly, and found a pair of posts I'd written two months apart about the same study, with the same evidence and a different opening. One did 15,186. The other did under 1,154.

This is what the difference was, what it cost me to find out I'd been wrong about my own best writing for a year, and the two things my data still cannot tell me.

What's the number in your own analytics that contradicts what you believe about your writing?

news.title: What to do before March
subjects: What to do before March
The door closes in about eighteen weeks. Then what?
Four things worth doing before the ban arrives
news.subtitle: The restriction is coming, and less changes in your house on the day than you think. Four things worth doing first.
news.body:
The Culture Secretary has named March 2027.

No exact date is official, the regulations that would fix it hadn't been laid when I wrote this, and official statements elsewhere still say spring. So call it roughly eighteen weeks, and hold it loosely.

And one thing is worth being clear about, because almost nobody says it out loud.

On the day it lands, nothing arrives for your child except a closed door.

What the ban does, and what it leaves exactly where it is

The three previous issues in this series went through this in detail, so I'll be brief.

A restriction changes access. Ofcom has named four ways of checking who is sixteen, and says plainly that no method is "completely robust against circumvention by children". Australia, three months into its own version, still had more than eight in ten of the relevant age group using at least one covered platform, and about half the children who still held accounts said the platform had never checked their age.

One thing did move there. Account ownership fell from 52.4 percent to 42.1 percent. That's real and it's the only measurable effect so far.

So the honest summary is that the door will mostly work, will not entirely work, and will not say a single word to your child about why it's there.

That's the gap. Eighteen weeks is how long you have to do something about it, and you do not need my product to use the time.

The mistake I'd most want you to avoid

The instinct, if you're the sort of parent who plans, is to treat March as a deadline to prepare for. Get ahead of it. Tighten up now so the transition is smooth.

I think that's backwards, and I've watched it go wrong.

If you take something away in November to get ahead of a rule that arrives in March, your child experiences a punishment with no cause. Nothing happened. They did nothing. The thing they enjoy went away because of a news story. And the lesson they take is not about judgement or safety. It's that access is arbitrary and the adult is the weather.

That matters because of the third readiness signal, the one I keep going on about: whether a child comes to you when something turns depends almost entirely on whether the last time went well enough that they'd do it again. A confiscation that your child experiences as unfair is a withdrawal from exactly the account you'll need in 2027.

So the four things below are all additions. None of them is a removal.

One. Find out what they actually use, not how long

Most parents, me included for years, know the number of hours and almost nothing else.

The useful inventory is different. Which apps. Which three people they talk to most. Which one thing they'd be most upset to lose. Whether anyone they talk to regularly is someone they've never met in person.

That last one is worth real attention. Ofcom's gaming research found that among children who game online, 55 percent at least sometimes play with people they've never met offline, while only 43 percent of parents set any rule about who their child plays with. Time limits ran at 56 percent. Those figures come from different questions and different groups so I won't turn them into a neat gap, but the direction is clear enough: we reach for the rule we can check.

Do this as curiosity, not audit. If it feels like an inspection you'll get an inspection's answers.

Time needed: one conversation, this week.

Two. Have the one conversation that isn't about rules

Ask why something is being shown to them.

Not "how long have you been on that". Not "who are you talking to". Just, pointing at whatever is on the screen, ask why they think it gave them that one.

I've come to think this is the single highest value thing a parent can do in this whole area, for a reason that took me a while to see. A child who can answer that question has a model of the thing they're using. A child who can't is inside something they experience as weather.

And it's a question you can ask fifty times without it becoming a row, because it isn't about them. It's about the machine.

If they say "because I watched one like it", that's a complete answer for a nine year old. If they're thirteen and the best they have is "it just does", you've learned where to start.

Time needed: thirty seconds, repeatedly, for the next eighteen weeks.

Three. Decide your own answer on the age check trade, before you're asked

Ofcom will consult on draft guidance once the regulations are laid. Parents are rarely the loudest voice in those, and the method is not settled.

The four on the table are a passport or licence upload, a reusable digital ID, a bank based check, and a facial age scan. Each asks your family for something different, and I went through the trades in the previous issue.

The thing to do now is pick one. Actually choose, in your own head, which you'd accept for your own child.

That sounds like homework with no reward. It isn't. An answer given during a consultation is worth considerably more than an objection raised after the system is built, and the people who will respond to that consultation with a settled view are mostly not parents.

Time needed: ten minutes, once, before the end of the year.

Four. Practise the handover, in the opposite direction from a ban

This is the one that takes the whole eighteen weeks, and it's the one a law can't touch.

A restriction removes a decision from a child. Every month between now and March, hand one back.

Not a big one. Something with a real consequence that's also survivable. Who they follow. When the device goes in the kitchen. Whether a group chat stays on overnight. Let them decide, let them get it wrong, and then do the hard part, which is not saying I told you so.

Because the ban guarantees one thing. At some point the door opens, whether that's at sixteen or on their eighteenth birthday or the first time they use someone else's login.

And on that day, the only thing standing between your child and the feed is the judgement they've practised.

A child who has never made a decision about this cannot start making good ones at sixteen. That's not a moral claim, it's just how practice works.

Time needed: one decision a month, handed over on purpose.

If your child is fourteen now

Everything above assumes you're preparing a child for something they haven't got yet. For a good number of you that isn't the situation, and I think this group has been almost entirely ignored in the coverage.

A child who's fourteen now will be fifteen when this lands. They already have the accounts. They already have the group chats, and in a lot of cases the friendships that live inside them. For them the restriction isn't a door that stays shut a bit longer. It's a removal.

That's a completely different experience and it deserves saying plainly: your child is likely to experience the ban as something being taken, by the government, for reasons they'll consider unfair, at the age when fairness matters most to them.

Two things follow.

The first is that you are not the author of this and you should say so, early and more than once. Not as a way of ducking it. Because a child who thinks you chose this will route around you, and a child who knows you didn't has somebody to be annoyed with it alongside. That distinction is worth more than any rule.

The second is more practical. If the accounts are going to close, the thing worth saving is the contact, not the content. A group chat that lives inside a covered platform disappears with the account. Phone numbers don't. Somewhere in the next eighteen weeks is a conversation about making sure the four or five friendships that actually matter have a route that survives March, and that conversation lands much better in January than in the week it happens.

I would not make that a project. I'd make it one remark, once, and let them do it themselves.

Where I should be careful, and am

I'd be a hypocrite if I spent three issues demanding proportionate claims and then sold you this as a programme.

So: none of the four is tested. I have no trial, no outcome data, and no evidence that a child who does these things behaves differently at sixteen from a child who doesn't. Nobody has that evidence, which is a problem with the field and not an excuse for me.

What I can tell you is that these are the actions I'd pick on the asymmetry argument. They're cheap if the effect of all this turns out to be small, which the evidence suggests it is. Taking a phone away for two years is expensive if the effect turns out to be small, because you've spent trust and taught nothing.

And there's one external support I'll lean on, lightly. The US National Academies committee that refused to conclude social media causes population level harm also recommended, in the same report, broader education for young people and training for the adults around them. That's not a vindication of my four things. It is the most cautious body in this field saying that teaching and adult capability belong in the response.

The thing I should say even though it isn't about screens

If you can only do one thing in the next eighteen weeks, and some weeks that's the honest situation, do the one that's about the relationship rather than the device.

The reason isn't sentimental. It's that the things which most strongly predict how a child's mental health goes are mostly not on the front page of the ban coverage: what the family is carrying, whether there's money, whether the adults are alright, whether help exists when it's needed. Social media sits a long way down that list.

A parent who gets the relationship slightly better has done more than a parent who gets the settings perfect. I've been both.

The ask, once

Our stage check is three questions about your own child and gives you a stage with the things worth practising next, which is the structured version of what I've described above. It's free and it takes a couple of minutes.

I'll say what I always say about it, because it would be strange to stop now. It's a starting point, not a measurement. We hold no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards, and almost nobody in this field does. If that admission costs me a subscriber, I'd rather lose the subscriber.

guidedchildhood.com, and the check is on the front.

What to do on Sunday

Do the second one. It's free, it takes thirty seconds, and it's the only one of the four that works at every age.

Sit down next to them while they're on something. Point at the screen. Ask why they think it gave them that one.

Then say nothing for ten seconds.

That pause is the hard part, and it's where the answer actually comes from.

What would your child say if you asked them that tonight?

The trial that is running right now, while the rest of us argue
What a randomised trial can settle, and what it cannot
news.subtitle: The protocol is public. Here is what it actually measures, what the children themselves asked for, and the question it was never built to answer.
news.body:
While we have been arguing about whether to limit children's social media, somebody has been quietly running the experiment.

The first wave of it finished about a week ago.

It is called the IRL Trial, it is based in Bradford, and its protocol is published. I have read it, all of it, and it is the most interesting document I have come across this year. Not because it settles the argument. Because of how carefully it refuses to pretend it can.

Here is what it does.

School year groups, not individual children, are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Both groups install the same app on their own phone. For one group the app limits social media to two hours a day and blocks it between nine at night and seven in the morning. For the other group the identical app only counts the hours and never stops anything. Six weeks. Then everybody answers the same questionnaire they answered at the start.

That design is the whole point, and it is worth slowing down on, because it is the thing almost no study in this field has.

Why this one is different from the studies we usually argue about

Nearly every number you have ever read about children and screens, including most of the ones I have written about, comes from asking a lot of children two questions at the same time and noticing that the answers move together. Children who use more social media report more anxiety. That is a real finding and it is reported honestly. It just cannot tell you which way round it runs.

It cannot tell you whether the scrolling made the child anxious, or the anxious child reached for the scrolling, or whether something else entirely, a hard year at home, a friendship that collapsed, a family under financial strain, produced both.

The trial's own protocol says this out loud, and I want to quote the sentence because of who is saying it. These are researchers who have staked years on finding an effect, writing in their own funding document:

the current observational evidence has several methodological limitations, including likely residual confounding and reverse causality, meaning the true effect of social media use on adolescent mental health is uncertain.

And then the line after it:

Scientific authorities in the UK and US have concluded that it is currently not possible to estimate the overall causal effect of digital technology on the wellbeing of children.

They are citing the National Academies consensus report and the UK Chief Medical Officers' own commentary. Which means the people running the biggest UK trial of social media limits began by writing down that nobody currently knows the answer.

That is not a weakness in their document. It is the reason the document exists.

A randomised trial fixes the direction problem by brute force. If you decide at random which year groups get the limit, then the only systematic difference between the two groups is the limit. Anything that shows up afterwards has an arrow pointing one way.

What it is actually measuring, which is narrower than the headlines will say

The primary outcome is anxiety. One thing. Measured with the anxiety subscale of a questionnaire called the RCADS-25: fifteen questions, each answered on a four point scale, producing a score from zero to forty five.

Depression and general wellbeing are secondary. Then there is a set of what the protocol calls mechanisms, which is the part I find most interesting: social media use itself, sleep, time spent with friends and family, and bullying. Those are the roads by which an effect, if there is one, would have to travel.

So when the result lands, the honest question is not "did it work". It is: did anxiety move, and if it did, did sleep or time with friends move with it in a way that explains how.

Two more numbers from the protocol that tell you how to read whatever comes out.

The trial is powered to detect a standardised effect of 0.16. That is the smallest effect it can reliably see. If the true effect is smaller than that, this trial will probably come back with nothing, and nothing will not mean zero. It will mean smaller than this trial could catch. I would like everybody who is going to write about the result to hold on to that sentence.

And the baseline anxiety score they are expecting, taken from Bradford data collected in 2023 and 2024, is 9.9 out of 45.

The children designed the intervention, and that changed it

This is the part of the protocol I did not expect.

The team consulted young people three times. In July 2025 they put seven options in front of 16 to 24 year olds, including phone abstinence and parental restrictions. The preference was clear: a restriction rather than a ban, delivered by an app the young person controlled. In December 2025 they asked 12 to 16 year olds about engagement, and got a strong preference for streaks, peer competition and notifications. In January 2026 another group said they would prefer an overnight restriction from nine until seven.

Every one of those preferences is in the final design. The two hour budget rather than a ban. The nine until seven curfew. The streaks and the leaderboards.

And one more thing, which I think is the most honest decision in the whole document. Participants can override the restrictions. They can push past the budget, and they can get in during the curfew. The app records it.

A lot of people will read that as a flaw. I read it as the researchers accepting that a limit a child cannot escape is not a limit, it is a confiscation, and that measuring what children do with a limit they can escape is the more useful question anyway.

They also left Year 7 out on purpose, and the reason is quietly damning. Under data protection law an eleven or twelve year old is not allowed a social media account at all, because the minimum age is thirteen. The team decided it would be uncomfortable for parents and teachers to enrol children in a social media study at an age when social media is not legally available to them.

Which would be fine, except that Bradford's own data says 86 percent of ten to twelve year olds already have a profile. The age rule has already failed for that group. The trial just cannot be the thing that says so.

The number I keep coming back to

While looking into this I found the companion paper, published in May 2026 by most of the same team, and it contains the most concrete estimate I have seen anybody put on this question.

They surveyed 8,466 Bradford students aged 12 to 15, weighted to the city. The median time on social media apps was 3.36 hours a day. Then they modelled what would happen if you capped it at three hours.

Their answer, and I want to give it to you exactly as they frame it: if the association were causal, capping daily use at three hours would reduce the share of children at clinical threshold for anxiety and depression symptoms from 10.7 percent to 9.5 percent. Which they then translate into the clearest sentence in this entire field.

Thirteen fewer cases in a typical school of a thousand pupils.

Hold that up against how this argument gets conducted. It is not nothing. Thirteen children in a school of a thousand is thirteen real children, and if your child is one of them you do not care what the aggregate looks like. It is also not a generation being rewired.

And the authors put the condition in the sentence themselves: "we cannot demonstrate strong evidence of a causal relationship". That is what the trial now running is for.

What it cannot tell you, and this is the part that matters at home

Six weeks of a two hour cap will tell us whether anxiety scores shift.

It will not tell you what a child does with the time. It will not tell you whether they moved to a different screen, which is in the protocol as a thing to watch and is the outcome I would bet on. It will not tell you anything about a nine year old, or about your child specifically, or about what happens in month seven.

And it cannot tell you the one thing I think actually decides how this goes for a family: whether the child understands why the limit exists.

A limit changes access. It does not teach judgement. If a child gets six quieter weeks and nothing happens in the quiet, they come out of it with the same instincts and a worse temper. If something does happen in the quiet, the six weeks were worth having whatever the anxiety score did.

Nobody can randomise that, which is exactly why it keeps falling out of the argument.

What to do this week

Borrow the design, not the result. The result is months away and may be modest.

Run the two hour budget and the nine until seven curfew in your own house for six weeks, with three conditions taken straight from the protocol.

One: the child can override it, and you both know they can. Build the override in deliberately. A limit your child has to break to escape teaches them to hide. A limit they can lift, and tell you they lifted, teaches them to notice. The trial made this choice on purpose and so should you.

Two: measure one thing, at the start and at the end. Not a feeling, something you can write down. What time they actually fell asleep. Or how many times that week they saw a friend in person. The trial picked sleep and time with friends and family as its mechanisms for a reason: they are the roads anything else would travel down. Pick one, write it on the back of an envelope now, look at it in six weeks.

Three: say out loud which of you chose this. The young people in the consultation did not ask for a ban. They asked for a restriction they controlled. That preference is worth taking seriously in your own kitchen, because a rule a teenager helped set is a different object from one that arrived.

Then at the end of the six weeks, ask the question the trial cannot: can they tell you, in their own words, what changed. That answer is worth more to you than the anxiety subscale, because it is about your child and the subscale is about four thousand of them.

If you want a starting point for where your own child is before you begin, our stage check is three questions and gives you a stage with the things worth practising next. It is a starting point, not a measurement, and I will not dress it up as more: we hold no evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards.

One last thing, about the waiting

The regulations that will restrict under sixteens in Britain are expected in spring 2027, with the Culture Secretary having named March, and no exact date officially confirmed.

The trial that is testing the thing being legislated is running right now. Its second wave finishes before Christmas. Nobody has published when it reports.

So we are going to legislate first and find out afterwards. I do not think that is a scandal, because governments cannot sit still waiting for perfect evidence about a risk they believe is real, and the trial team says as much themselves.

But it does mean something for you. The law will arrive on a date somebody chose. The evidence will arrive on a date nobody has announced. What happens in your house between now and then is not waiting on either of them.

Sources, and what each one can carry

Sources, and what each one can carry

The IRL Trial protocol, version 1.3, 12 August 2026, published by Born in Bradford. Read in full for this issue. Everything about the design comes from here: the cluster randomisation of year groups, the two hour daily budget, the nine until seven curfew, the six week period, the override, the anxiety primary outcome measured on the RCADS-25 anxiety subscale, the secondary outcomes, the mechanisms, the 0.16 powered effect size, the baseline score of 9.9 out of 45, the exclusion of Year 7 and its reason, the three young people's consultations and their dates, and the two quoted sentences about observational evidence and about what scientific authorities have concluded.

The trial's governance, from the same protocol. Co principal investigators Dr Dan Lewer at Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and Professor Amy Orben at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit, Cambridge. Sponsor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust. Funded by both the Wellcome Trust and the National Institute for Health Research, which I had previously described as Wellcome alone, and that was incomplete. A partnership with the University of Cambridge and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine Clinical Trials Unit, which runs the primary analysis.

Scale. Born in Bradford's public page says 4,000 students in years 8 to 10 across secondary schools in the city. The protocol is more precise and slightly larger: to detect its target effect the trial needs 30 year groups, about 10 schools and roughly 4,500 participants, and it aims to recruit 12 schools to allow for one or two dropping out. Where the two differ I have used the protocol.

Timeline. The protocol gives two waves: 1 September 2026 to the autumn half term, and after half term finishing before Christmas 2026. No published reporting date for the results exists. I have now looked for one across three sessions and in the protocol itself. The protocol says the team will pre register their analyses but gives no registration number. If you see anybody claim a results date, ask them where it came from.

The Bradford survey, for the three hour cap estimate: Pickavance, O'Nions, Hammad, Jackson, Lightfoot, McEachan, Orben, Ryan, Shire, Wood, Wright and Lewer, "Adolescent social media use and its association with mental health: a cross sectional study in Bradford, England", BMC Public Health, 7 May 2026. 8,466 students aged 12 to 15 from Born in Bradford: Age of Wonder 2023 to 2024, weighted to the city's 12 to 15 year old population. Median 3.36 hours a day, interquartile range 1.88 to 5.44. The reduction from 10.7 percent to 9.5 percent, and the thirteen children per thousand, are the paper's own figures under its own stated assumption that the association is causal, which the paper says it cannot demonstrate. It is a cross sectional study. It cannot establish cause, and it says so.

The 86 percent of ten to twelve year olds in Bradford with their own social media profile is cited in the trial protocol to Ofcom's Children and Parents: Media Use and Attitudes Report 2025. I have not read the Ofcom report directly, because Ofcom's site refuses the tools I use.

The ban date. The Culture Secretary has named March 2027 and the Commons statement and Hansard say spring 2027. Smartphone Free Childhood's own parent guidance says no exact date is officially confirmed. The regulations that would fix it were due to be laid before the end of 2026 and had not been laid when I wrote this.

What I have not claimed. No result from this trial, because there isn't one. No reporting date. No outcome for any child from anything we build.

news.title: The arrows that survived point the other way
subjects: Twenty five thousand children, one question about hours, and nothing
The arrows that survived point the other way
The study that clears social media also shows why we keep measuring it wrong
news.subtitle: The best designed UK study on this found no evidence that social media predicts later distress. It also measured social media with a single question about hours. Both of those things are true and they belong in the same issue.
news.body:
A study of 25,629 teenagers in Greater Manchester found no evidence that time spent on social media predicted later emotional difficulties. Not for girls. Not for boys. Gaming the same.

I want to take this one seriously, because it cuts against things I have said.

And then I want to show you the single question the study used to measure social media, because it changes what the finding means without making it any less true.

What they did, and why the design is the interesting part

The team is at the University of Manchester, working with colleagues at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, and they used the #BeeWell cohort: children across Greater Manchester surveyed each autumn, in 2021, 2022 and 2023.

The sample is unusually good for this field. Average age twelve years and seven months at the start. Fifty one percent girls. Seventeen percent with special educational needs, twenty nine percent eligible for free school meals, thirty four percent from minoritised ethnic groups. That last set of numbers matters, because a recurring and fair complaint about this literature is that it runs on small, comfortable, homogeneous samples. This one does not.

One correction before I go on, and it is a correction to myself.

I wrote earlier that the study followed the same children for three years. It is more complicated than that, and the paper is straight about it. The team used what they call a drop in approach, including any participant with at least one of the three data points, and the methods section describes the final sample as 25,629 observations rather than 25,629 children measured three times each. Another 2,620 were excluded for missing covariates.

I took the looser version from the university's own press release, which says the team "followed young people aged 11-14 over three school years". That is the release being less careful than the paper. I will come back to that, because it turns out to be the story.

Now the design. It is called a random intercept cross lagged panel model, which is an ugly name for a genuinely clever idea.

Picture two questions you could ask about the same data. The first: do children who use more social media tend to be more distressed than other children? The second: when a particular child uses more social media than that child usually does, does that child become more distressed afterwards than they usually are?

Almost every study you have read answers the first question and gets reported as though it answered the second. They are not the same question. The first compares children to each other, so it picks up everything that makes children different, including the home they live in, the money in it, and what has happened to them. The second compares a child to themselves, which strips most of that out.

This model separates the two. And when it does, here is what happens.

At the between person level, comparing children to each other, there is a small but statistically significant positive correlation. Children who use more social media do report more emotional difficulty. That finding survives.

At the within person level, following the same child over time, it goes. Social media use in one year did not predict emotional difficulties the next, for girls or for boys. Gaming did not either. The authors ran it again splitting active use from passive scrolling, and got the same answer.

So the honest summary is not "no link". It is: the link between children is real, and the link within a child, across a year, is not there. Which is exactly what you would expect if something about a child's life were producing both.

The two arrows that did survive, and they point backwards

This is the part almost nobody has reported, and it is the most interesting thing in the paper.

Two effects did clear the bar the authors set for themselves.

For girls, more gaming in year two predicted less time on social media in year three. For boys, more emotional difficulty in year two predicted less gaming in year three, an effect the paper says met a lower bound of 0.10 and was therefore "likely meaningful".

Read that second one again. Feeling worse came first, and the gaming went down afterwards. The direction we spend all our time arguing about ran the other way.

The paper's co author Professor Neil Humphrey put it plainly in the release: young people's choices around social media and gaming "may be shaped by how they're feeling but not necessarily the other way around."

I do not think that means the worry is misplaced. I think it means a teenager who goes quiet and stops playing the game they loved is telling you something, and a parent watching the clock will read it as good news.

The sentence that is doing the work, and the one question underneath it

Here is how the study measured social media use. One question, adapted from the Millennium Cohort Study:

On a normal weekday during term time, how much time do you spend on social media?

With an example, "sites or apps like TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat", and answers in hourly bands from zero to seven or more.

Gaming was one question too. How often do you play games on a computer or console, with six options collapsed down to four: rarely, occasionally, sometimes, often.

That is it. That is the exposure.

Now, I am not sneering at it. Single item measures from a validated national cohort are standard, the alternative is asking twenty five thousand children to install tracking software, and the authors name self report as a limitation themselves: social media and gaming here "do not capture an objective assessment nor a nuanced reflection of these constructs".

But look at what that question can and cannot see.

It cannot see who the child was talking to. It cannot see whether the hour was spent building something with a school friend or being slowly frozen out of a group chat. It cannot see a feed narrowing. It cannot see one message at eleven at night that the child is still carrying at breakfast. A child who had the worst evening of their year and a child who had a lovely one both answer "two hours".

So the finding, stated as precisely as I can manage, is this: self reported hours on a normal weekday do not predict a child's emotional difficulties a year later.

That is a real result and it is bad news for anybody whose argument runs on hours. It is also not the same sentence as "social media is not affecting children", and the gap between those two sentences is where the press release went.

Where the release went further than the paper

The paper's conclusion reads: the findings "do not support the widely held view that adolescent technology use is a major causal factor in their mental health difficulties". In the discussion, the authors say these activities "may not play a causal role".

May not. A lack of evidence for a thing, carefully stated.

The university's release, published on 14 January 2026, is headlined "Time spent on gaming and social media not to blame for teen mental health issues". The opening line says there is little evidence that social media and gaming "are causing" mental health problems. Another line says technology habits "did not appear to drive" difficulties.

Not to blame. Are causing. Those are claims about the world. "May not play a causal role" is a claim about the evidence. The distance between them is small enough to miss and large enough to matter, and it is the distance that the headline travelled.

To be fair to the release, it does carry the caveats. It says plainly that this does not mean online experiences are harmless, and that hurtful messages, online pressures and extreme content can all have real impacts on wellbeing. It mentions both of the backwards arrows. Lead author Dr Qiqi Cheng is quoted saying the results do not support the idea that simply spending time on these things leads to mental health problems, and then adds, "the story is far more complex than that".

That is a good release with a headline that undoes part of it. Which is how most of them work, and why I would rather read the paper.

And I am in no position to be smug, since I repeated the release's description of the sample without checking it against the methods. The thing I am complaining about is the thing I did.

What a parent actually takes from this

Three things, and then one to do this week.

The hours are not the signal. The best designed study we have, on the biggest and most mixed UK sample, looked at hours and found nothing predictive. If you have been keeping score on the clock and feeling like you are failing, you have been grading yourself on a measure that the evidence does not support. You can put that down.

A withdrawal is a signal. The one effect in this paper that was likely meaningful was boys who felt worse playing less afterwards. Stopping is data.

The fight was never really about the hours. Mine wasn't. The argument in my house was about the thing in my son's hand that kept asking for him back, and about what happened in his head afterwards. No clock reaches that.

The thing to do this week

Swap one question for three. Instead of "how long have you been on that", which the evidence now says is close to useless as a predictor, ask the three things that single survey question could not see.

Who were you talking to. Not an interrogation, a normal question asked normally, the way you would ask who they sat with at lunch.

What did it leave you with. The study measured emotional difficulties a year later. You can ask about ten minutes later, which is a thing no researcher can do and you can do tonight.

Did anything happen that you nearly told me about. This is the one that matters, and it is not really a question about the phone. It is a question about whether coming to you went well enough last time that they would do it again.

Ask one of the three. Not all three, not as a list, and not tonight if tonight is already difficult. One, asked lightly, and then stop talking.

If you want a starting point for where your own child is, our stage check is three questions and gives you a stage with the things worth practising next. It is a starting point and not a measurement, and I will not pretend otherwise: we hold no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards, and almost nobody in this field does.

The thing I keep coming back to

Twenty five thousand children, three years, one of the better designed studies in the field, and the answer to "do the hours predict the misery" is no.

I believe that result. I also think it has cleared away the wrong question, which leaves the real one standing in the open where everybody can see it.

Not how long. What, and who with, and what happened after.

Sources, and what each one can carry

Sources, and what each one can carry

The paper. Qiqi Cheng, Margarita Panayiotou, Turi Reiten Finserås, Amanda Iselin Olesen Andersen and Neil Humphrey, "How do social media use, gaming frequency, and internalizing symptoms predict each other over time in early to middle adolescence?", Journal of Public Health, volume 48, issue 1, March 2026, pages 59 to 69, doi 10.1093/pubmed/fdaf150. Cheng, Panayiotou and Humphrey are at the Manchester Institute of Education, University of Manchester; Finserås and Andersen at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health in Bergen. Read in full from the primary PDF for this issue, which is why this issue can quote the measures and the methods rather than the summary of them.

Everything here comes from that document: the three waves in the autumns of 2021, 2022 and 2023; the drop in approach including any participant with at least one data point; the 25,629 observations in the main analytical model and the 2,620 excluded; the demographic breakdown; the random intercept cross lagged panel model and what it separates; the between person positive correlations; the absence of within person prediction in either direction for either sex; the active versus passive sensitivity analysis; the two surviving backwards effects and the 0.07 and 0.10 benchmarks they were judged against; and both quoted conclusions.

The measures, quoted exactly: the social media item and the gaming item are both single items adapted from the Millennium Cohort Study, and internalising symptoms were the ten item emotional difficulties subscale of the Me and My Feelings measure, with internal consistency of 0.88, 0.89 and 0.90 across the three waves.

The limitation I lean on is the authors' own, and I am not using it against them. They write that social media and gaming are both self reported and "do not capture an objective assessment nor a nuanced reflection of these constructs".

The press release. University of Manchester, "Time spent on gaming and social media not to blame for teen mental health issues", 14 January 2026, read in full. Every quoted phrase from it is verbatim. The release was published around thirteen months after the paper first appeared online and in the run up to the March 2026 print issue, which is why coverage of this study clusters in January 2026 while the paper is dated 2026.

One date I will not pin. The paper's own front matter and the journal's article page give different online publication dates for it. I have not been able to reconcile them, so this issue gives the print issue, March 2026, which both agree on, and nothing more precise.

What this issue does not claim. That social media is harmless, which neither the paper nor the release says. That the study measured anything other than self reported hours and frequency. Any outcome for any child from anything we build.

news.title: The thing parents want least is the thing being sold
subjects: The thing parents want least from an AI toy is the thing being sold
A teddy bear, a banned developer, and three months later
Half the children in the country have one, and almost nobody is checking
news.subtitle: Parents rank companionship last among everything they want from an AI toy. Companionship is the category. Here is what two teams found when they actually tested them, and the enforcement gap underneath.
news.body:
Ask parents what they want an AI toy to do for their child and they put companionship last. Dead last, out of seven options, on 22 percent. More than half say they actively do not want these things acting as a friend or providing emotional comfort.

Now look at what is being sold. The category is called AI companion toys.

That gap is the story, and it is a more useful story than the one in the headlines, because it is not about whether the toys are evil. It is about a product being built to do the one job its buyers put at the bottom of the list.

Half of UK children have already been given one.

The numbers, and whose they are

I want to be careful here, because the good research on this is American and the UK number is thin, and those two facts get blended in most coverage.

The UK figure. A survey of 1,000 UK parents, carried out by FocalData in May 2026 and published by the British Standards Institution, found parents reporting that around half of their children have been given an AI toy or learning device, and that 38 percent own two or more. It is a parent survey, so it is what parents report rather than what children do, and "AI enabled toy or learning device" is a wide box that holds a spelling tutor and a talking bear in the same hand. I have not read the underlying data, only the published summary. And the headline the BSI itself drew from it was not that children are in danger. It was that guidance for the adults buying these things barely exists.

The American figures are better and are not ours. Common Sense Media surveyed 1,004 US adults in a poll weighted to represent American adults, and separately sat down and tested three of these toys. Both reports are published and I have read both.

From the survey:

- 49 percent of parents have bought or are considering an AI enabled toy or device. 43 percent do not own one and do not intend to. - 83 percent are concerned about these toys collecting their child's personal information. It is the single highest concern they measured. - Then setting usage limits and cybersecurity, both on 79 percent. Then the toy saying something inappropriate, on 74 percent. Then less time playing with friends and family, 64 percent. - What parents actually want: helping their child learn, 70 percent. Encouraging good manners, 62 percent. Practising conversation and social skills, 51 percent. Imaginative play, 40 percent. Monitoring the child when the parent is out of the room, 37 percent. Something to do independently, 35 percent. - Companionship, 22 percent. Last. - Only 19 percent would at least somewhat like an AI companion for their child. 56 percent say they do not want one acting as a companion or giving emotional comfort. Among parents of nought to four year olds, 84 percent express little or no interest in that.

One more from that survey which I did not expect, and which I think deserves more attention than it will get. Uptake is highest among Black parents, at 78 percent bought or considering, against 61 percent of Hispanic parents and 36 percent of White parents. And future interest is highest in households earning under fifty thousand dollars, at 65 percent, against 39 percent of the highest earners.

So the families most likely to bring one of these into the house are, on average, the ones with the least slack to absorb it going wrong. That pattern is familiar from every other technology I write about, and it is the reason I do not think "just do not buy one" is an answer.

What happened when somebody tested them

Common Sense Media's researchers tested three toys, Grem, Bondu and Miko 3, using child accounts with stated ages from six to thirteen, talking to them out loud the way a child would.

Their finding: 27 percent of outputs were inappropriate for children. More than a quarter. The report lists the categories, and they are not all the same thing: mature topics, inappropriate boundaries, risky advice, unsafe roleplay.

Their recommendation is flat. They do not recommend AI toys for children aged five and under at all, and they urge caution for six to twelve.

They also found something less dramatic and, if you have ever handed a device to a small child, more recognisable. The toys are glitchy. They activate when nobody meant them to and miss it when a child is actually talking to them.

I should name a disclosure the organisation makes about itself, because it cuts both ways and leaving it out would be the kind of thing I complain about in other people. Common Sense Media's institute says it is funded by both philanthropy and industry, including the makers of some of the technologies it evaluates. You can read that as a conflict or as unusual candour. Either way you should know it.

The part that actually changed my mind

A second team, the PIRG Education Fund, published in March 2026, and their report is not really about toys. It is about whether anybody is enforcing anything.

Last autumn they bought a scarf wearing teddy bear called Kumma, made by a Singapore based company, FoloToy. It talked, over wifi, powered by a commercial chatbot. Some of the conversations were what you would expect from a talking bear, favourite school subjects, games to play. Others were not. The bear gave their researchers step by step instructions for lighting a match, and produced explicit sexual content.

The bear was marketed as running on OpenAI's GPT-4o, and ran on it by default.

Then the system worked, briefly and visibly. The day after PIRG published, FoloToy suspended all sales of its products pending a safety audit. OpenAI said it had banned the company from using its models.

Here is what PIRG found when they went back in February 2026, more than three months after that ban was announced. Mentions of the old model had been scrubbed from FoloToy's website. But a newer OpenAI model was still selectable in the portal where you choose what powers the toy, and PIRG could still use their Kumma apparently set to it. They sent OpenAI the documentation and asked whether the company knew. OpenAI reiterated that FoloToy was banned.

Banned, and still working. Three months later.

PIRG tested another toy too, the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, and concluded that both it and the Kumma had safeguards inadequate enough that a toy meant for young children could be made to discuss explicit topics. They also report multiple apparent breaches of Google's rule against using its models in children's products.

And on the 83 percent of parents worried about data collection: PIRG reports that Bondu, one of the toys in the other team's test, exposed 50,000 lines of dialogue that children had exchanged with it, sitting in an unprotected database.

What I think this adds up to

Not that AI toys are a catastrophe. I am not going to tell you that, because the evidence does not support it and because a spelling tutor and a bear that wants to be your child's confidant are different products with the same label on the shelf.

What it adds up to is that the safety question has moved. For years the question about children's products has been "is there a rule". For these, the rule existed. A company published developer policies. A developer broke them. The developer was publicly banned. And three months later the toy still worked.

So the real question is "who is checking", and the honest answer from both of these reports is that nobody much is, and that the companies have decided developer responsibility is a sufficient answer. One of the AI toy makers' own chief executives would presumably say they are a small part of a large ecosystem. Common Sense put it more sharply: most toys face rigorous safety testing before they reach the market, and we still lack meaningful child safeguards for AI.

The other thing it adds up to is the gap I opened with. A toy that answers every question, never gets tired and never says "not now" is teaching a child something about what a relationship is. Parents can see that, which is why companionship came last and why 84 percent of parents of under fives want nothing to do with it.

A seven year old cannot see it for themselves. That is not a failing in the seven year old.

What to do this week

If one of these is already in your house, or is about to arrive at Christmas, there are two jobs and only one of them is about the toy.

The job that is about the toy: find out what it keeps. Not what it says, what it keeps. Open the app or the web portal it came with and look for three things. Whether there is a transcript of what your child has said to it, and whether you can read it. Whether you can delete it. And which company's model is actually behind it, which is often a dropdown in a portal and is the exact thing PIRG found had not been cleaned up. Twenty minutes, once. If you cannot find out what it keeps, you have learnt something.

The job that is about the child, which matters more. Four things a child should be able to tell you, in their own words, about anything in the house that talks back.

Who is on the other side of this. Not "a robot", something closer to: it is a computer program made by a company, and there is nobody in there.

What it remembers. Children assume either nothing or everything. Both are wrong, and the true answer is one you will have had to look up yourself, which is why the first job comes first.

What it cannot do. It cannot be sad for them. It cannot keep a secret in any way that means anything. It does not know if they are telling the truth.

When to go and find a person. This is the only one that counts if the others fail.

A child who can say those four things back to you has something an age limit on a box cannot give them, and something no enforcement regime currently delivers either. We teach a short lesson on exactly this for younger children, and it starts from the idea that the child should be able to explain it to you rather than recite it.

And if the toy has not arrived yet: 22 percent. Companionship came last on the list of things parents want. If you are buying, buy the one that teaches something.

One last thought for the people buying presents

The age on the box is a manufacturing claim. It is not a finding about your child, and after reading both of these reports I do not think it is a finding about the toy either.

Nobody has told most parents what to look for. That was the British Standards Institution's own conclusion from its UK survey, and it is the most useful sentence in any of this.

So the four questions are not a precaution. For now they are the guidance.

Sources, and what each one can carry

Sources, and what each one can carry

Common Sense Media, "AI in the Toy Box", the parent survey. Read in full from the primary PDF. The method, in its own terms: a web survey of US adults aged 18 or older, 951 in English and 53 in Spanish, so 1,004 in total, weighted to represent that population. Every percentage in the survey section above is from this document: the 49 and 43 percent on purchase, the 83 percent on personal information and its place as the highest measured concern, the 79, 79, 74 and 64 percent concerns, the full priority list down to companionship at 22 percent, the 19 percent who would like a companion and the 56 percent who would not, the 84 percent of parents of nought to four year olds, and the breakdowns by ethnicity and household income. This is American data about American parents. None of it is UK data and I would not carry the percentages across.

Common Sense Media, "AI Risk Assessment: AI Toys", dated 14 January 2026. Read in full from the primary PDF. The three toys tested were Grem, Bondu and Miko 3, using child accounts with stated ages from 6 to 13, interacting by voice. The 27 percent of outputs judged inappropriate, and the categories listed, are from this document, as is the age guidance in its own wording: it does not recommend AI toys for children aged 5 and under and urges caution for 6 to 12. The organisation's disclosure that its institute is funded by both philanthropy and industry, including makers of technologies it evaluates, is its own.

One limit on the 27 percent. The report does not give the total number of outputs tested, so I cannot tell you 27 percent of how many. Treat it as a proportion of a test set of unstated size, from three products, not as a population estimate.

PIRG Education Fund, "Not for kids. Found in toys: How AI companies' loose rules for developers put kids at risk", March 2026, with the follow up testing done in February 2026. Read in full from the primary PDF. The Kumma account, the FoloToy suspension and OpenAI's ban, the newer model still being selectable and usable three months later, OpenAI's response, the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, the apparent breaches of Google's developer rule, and the 50,000 lines of children's dialogue exposed by Bondu are all from this report.

The UK figure is the weakest thing in this issue and I have said so in the text. FocalData, 1,000 UK parents, May 2026, published by the British Standards Institution: around half of children given an AI toy or learning device, 38 percent with two or more. I have the published summary and not the underlying tables. It is a parent report, not an observation of children, and the category is broad.

What this issue does not claim. That AI toys harm children, which none of these documents establishes and none of them claims. That the American percentages apply to British families. Any outcome for any child from anything we build. I have also not described the explicit content these reports found in any more detail than naming it, because the detail adds nothing a parent needs.

news.title: The rules are being written for the eight percent
subjects: The rules are being written for the eight percent
Four in five children use the thing nobody is regulating
Homework help, and where it goes next
news.subtitle: Australia asked 1,950 children about AI. Almost all of them use an assistant. Almost none use a companion. Nearly every law being drafted is about the companion.
news.body:
Australia's online safety regulator asked 1,950 children aged ten to seventeen about artificial intelligence. Seventy eight percent had used an AI assistant. Eight percent had used an AI companion.

Now count the laws.

New York has passed one limiting what a chatbot may do with a minor. California's companion chatbot law took effect at the start of this year. Idaho, Oregon and Washington have acted on chatbots claiming to be conscious and on sexual conversations with minors. Georgia has restricted relationship simulation features for under eighteens. A federal bill in the United States would bar minors from AI companions altogether and has cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Nearly all of it is aimed at the companion. The eight percent.

And the tool that four children in five are actually using is the ordinary assistant, the one most parents have filed under homework help.

Before I go further, what I can and cannot stand behind

I am going to be unusually blunt about the evidence in this issue, because it is the weakest in this series and you should know that before you read the argument.

eSafety's report is called "Talking to machines", it was released on 3 August 2026, and I have not read it. Its site has refused the tools I use four times now, across three separate attempts over two weeks. So have the mirrors.

What that means in practice:

- The headline figures, the 78 percent and the 8 percent, are confirmed through eSafety's own published summary and media release and are consistent everywhere I find them. I am comfortable with those. - The figure I would most like to use, that 54 percent of children who had used an assistant or a companion said they used it for personal or social reasons, I am giving you with a warning rather than confidence. I have never seen the question the children were asked. "Personal or social" is a wide bucket. It could be a chat about a game as easily as a worry. Until somebody reads me the question, treat that number as a direction and not a measurement. - Figures I have seen reported but will not build an argument on: that about one in five children who used either tool reported a potentially inappropriate or harmful interaction, and that around one in three shared personal or sensitive information. Both come to me through summaries rather than the document. They are almost certainly roughly right. I just will not lean on a number I have not read.

These are also Australian children, not British ones, and I would not carry the percentages across.

What does carry across is the shape. And the shape is the whole point.

Two countries, two surveys, the same shape

Set the Australian figures beside an American one.

The Pew Research Center surveyed 1,458 American teenagers aged thirteen to seventeen in the autumn of 2025. Fifty four percent had used a chatbot for help with schoolwork. Twelve percent had asked one for emotional support or advice.

Different country, different question, different year. Same shape. Overwhelming use of the general purpose tool, a much smaller slice using it for something personal, and almost nobody describing a dedicated companion app as their main experience.

Two independent samples landing on the same structure is worth more than either on its own, and it tells you something that neither headline does.

The exposure is not concentrated in a product category. It is spread across a tool that looks harmless.

Why that matters more than it sounds

If you are writing a rule, a product category is a wonderful thing to have. It has a name. You can define it, require an age check on it, and tell a parent to look for it. Everything about it is enforceable.

A general purpose assistant is the opposite. It is on the phone already. It is on the laptop the school handed out. It is inside the search box, the word processor and increasingly the operating system. There is no aisle it sits in.

So a rule about companion apps is not wrong, and I want to be fair about this. The worst documented cases, the ones that have driven the legislation, involve companion products designed to hold a young person's attention and simulate a relationship. Those products deserve the scrutiny. A law that makes them harder for a fourteen year old to reach is a reasonable thing for a legislature to do.

It just will not touch the thing most children are doing.

And here is the part I find genuinely difficult. A general purpose assistant is also the one with the better guardrails, the bigger safety team and the stronger commercial reason not to produce a disaster. The companion app with nobody checking it is both more dangerous per child and used by far fewer of them.

Both things being true at once is why this is hard, and why I distrust anybody who finds it easy.

The part of this no ban can reach

There is one more reason the companion category is the easy target and the assistant is the hard one, and it is the reason I think almost nothing being drafted will touch the actual exposure.

A lot of children meet their first AI assistant at school.

Not through a product their parents bought or a app they downloaded, but on a device the school issued, inside software the school chose, with an assistant built into the word processor or the learning platform or the search box. In that setting the use is not only permitted, it is instructed. The child is being taught to use it, graded on work produced alongside it, and told by an adult that this is the right tool for the job.

Every protective instinct we have about children and technology assumes a parent can decide. Buy it or do not. Allow the app or do not. Set the limit or do not.

None of that applies to a tool that arrives with the homework.

And it means the conversation a child has with an assistant at four in the afternoon, about a piece of coursework, on a school laptop, sits entirely outside the reach of an age restriction, a parental control and a family rule. It is also the single most common way children in this country are currently encountering these systems.

I am not saying schools should not use them. The better ones are being thoughtful about it, and a child who learns to use a powerful tool well under supervision is in a better position than one who meets it alone at thirteen. I am saying that if you are a parent trying to work out where to put your attention, the answer is not the thing with an age rating. It is the thing with a login your child was given.

The finding I keep returning to

Of the children who had used either tool, the Australian survey reports that somewhere around half had taken it somewhere personal or social.

I have told you why I hold that number loosely. But even at half the size it would still say something, and it fits what the American data shows at a lower number for a narrower question.

A meaningful minority of children are not using these things as a calculator. They are using them as somebody to talk to. And the one they are talking to is mostly not the product built to be talked to. It is the homework tool.

There are two readings of that and I hold both on different days.

The first is that a child typing a worry into a machine late at night is a child who did not have, or did not trust, a person to tell. On that reading the machine is a symptom, and one that is built to keep a conversation going.

The second is that for some young people, saying a thing out loud to something with no face is a way of practising. Rehearsing the sentence before they say it to a person. That is not nothing, and I have watched an adult do exactly that.

No survey can tell you which. Nobody has followed these children long enough to find out.

What I think it comes down to is not whether the tool is safe. It is whether the conversation ends with a person, or ends with another conversation.

The finding nobody is legislating

One more thing from the Australian work, reported in its summary rather than read by me, and it is the most actionable item in this entire issue.

Very few children knew how to report a problem. And parents' awareness dropped sharply for companions compared with assistants.

Think about what that means next to everything above. The regulatory energy is going into keeping children away from one category. Meanwhile the children who are already in the other category, in enormous numbers, mostly cannot tell you what to do when something goes wrong inside it.

Engagement with companions was also reported as higher among children with a disability or a diagnosed mental health condition. If that holds, the children most likely to form an attachment to one are the children already carrying something, which is the pattern that runs through every topic I write about and the reason I keep saying the average child is not the story.

What to do this week

Two things, and the second one takes ten minutes and almost nobody has done it.

First, find out which one it is. Not whether your child uses AI, they almost certainly do. Which kind. The question that gets you a real answer is not "do you use ChatGPT", it is "what did you last ask it". A homework answer and a question about a friendship are different houses to be living in, and you cannot tell from the outside.

Ask it in the car, or while doing something else, and then do not react to the first answer. The first answer is a test.

Second, find the report button together. This is the one.

Open the assistant your child actually uses. Not a companion app, the real one, the one on their phone or their school laptop. Then the two of you find out, together, what happens when something it says is wrong or frightening. Is there a thumbs down. Does it go anywhere. Is there a way to flag a conversation. Can you see the history, and can you delete it.

You are not doing this to install a safeguard. You are doing it so that the answer to "what do I do if this gets weird" is something your child has already done once, with you, on an ordinary afternoon, rather than something they have to work out alone at eleven at night.

If you cannot find a route, that is worth knowing too, and worth saying out loud to your child: this thing you talk to has no good way for you to tell anybody when it goes wrong, so I am the route.

That sentence is the whole lesson, and it does not depend on which country's survey you believe.

Where I have landed

A rule written for companion apps misses the tool nearly four children in five actually use. That is not an argument against the rule. It is an argument against mistaking the rule for the answer.

And the habit that carries across every country, every product category and every version of the law is the same one: knowing who is on the other side, and knowing when to stop talking to a machine and go and find a person.

We teach a short lesson on exactly that for younger children, and it starts from the idea that the child should be able to explain it to you. If you want a starting point for where your own child is, our stage check is three questions and returns a stage with the things worth practising next. A starting point, not a measurement. We hold no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards.

Sources, and what each one can carry

Sources, and what each one can carry

This is the least well sourced issue in this series and the text says so twice.

eSafety Commissioner (Australia), "Talking to machines: Children's experiences with AI assistants and companions", released 3 August 2026. An online survey of 1,950 children aged 10 to 17, fielded between 2 February and 4 March 2026.

I have not read this report. esafety.gov.au has returned a server error to our tools on four attempts across three sessions, including to the direct PDF link, and the Analysis and Policy Observatory mirror refuses us as well. Everything attributed to it here comes from eSafety's own research landing page and media release plus consistent secondary reporting.

Of its figures:

- 78 percent had used an AI assistant and 8 percent had used an AI companion, both of all children surveyed. Confirmed in multiple independent places and used with confidence. - 54 percent used it for personal or social reasons, among children who had used an assistant or a companion rather than among all children. Used in this issue with an explicit warning, because the question wording and response options are still unread. This is the fifth time I have tried to get at that question. - Around 20 percent of users on it daily or more, reported in the summary. - About one in five users reporting a potentially inappropriate or harmful interaction, and around one in three sharing personal or sensitive information. Named in the issue as reported figures I will not build on. - Higher companion engagement among children with disability or a diagnosed mental health condition, and the findings on children not knowing how to report and on lower parental awareness of companions. All from summaries. Treated as reported rather than established, and labelled that way in the text.

Pew Research Center, 1,458 American teenagers aged 13 to 17, surveyed in autumn 2025: 54 percent had used a chatbot for schoolwork, 12 percent for emotional support or advice. American teenagers, not British ones. Note that the 54 percent here and the 54 percent in the Australian survey are different figures about different things and should never be put in the same sentence without this explanation, which is exactly the mistake I would expect coverage to make.

The legislation. New York's law limiting chatbot features for minors; California's companion chatbot law, reported as effective 1 January 2026; laws in Idaho, Oregon and Washington on chatbots claiming sentience and on sexual conversations with minors; Georgia's restrictions on relationship simulation features for minors; and a federal bill that would bar minors from AI companions, reported as approved by the Senate Judiciary Committee. All of this is American and I have checked none of it against the statutes. Dates and status in the reporting I found were inconsistent, so I have named what each law does in general terms and given a date only where I found one stated. I found nothing comparable to cite for the United Kingdom or the European Union, which is itself worth knowing.

What this issue does not claim. That AI assistants harm children. That the Australian percentages describe British children. Any specific harm figure as established. Any outcome for any child from anything we build.

news.title: The one number that measures something, and nobody quotes it
subjects: Both sides are quoting the same paper to prove opposite things
The one number that measures something, and nobody quotes it
What would actually change your mind about the ban
news.subtitle: A study everyone quoted said 85 percent of Australian teenagers got round the ban. It doesn't say that. And the regulator's own figure, the only one that measures anything, is missing from both arguments.
news.body:
A study everyone was quoting a few weeks ago said that 85 percent of Australian teenagers got round the under sixteen social media ban.

It doesn't say that.

What it says is that more than 85 percent of under sixteens were still using the platforms three months after the ban began, mostly on accounts they already had.

Still using is not the same as broke in. One describes a door being forced. The other describes a door that was never shut behind the people already inside.

That distinction is not pedantry, and I am going to spend this issue on it, because the way this one paper has been used tells you almost everything about how the argument over children and phones is now conducted. Both sides are quoting it. Both sides are quoting it for things it does not say. And the single number in this whole story that actually measures the effect of the ban is being quoted by neither.

What the paper is, and what it found

The study is in the BMJ, from a team at the University of Newcastle in Australia. It recruited 436 adolescents and followed up with 408 of them three months after the ban came into force.

Its finding on continued use is the 85 percent figure, and the crucial detail is the mechanism: most of those still using were on accounts that already existed before the ban. The platforms did not let them back in. The platforms never removed them.

The paper also says, in its own terms, that there is not enough evidence of a real drop in use. And its authors say the full picture may take a decade.

One Australian state. Self reported answers. Four hundred and eight young people.

A good, careful, small study of the first three months of a policy that will take years to assess, which has been handed a job it cannot do.

The number that measures something

Now the regulator's own follow up, which surveyed 803 children.

The share of children who actually held an account on an age restricted platform fell from 52.4 percent to 42.1 percent. eSafety describes that change as modest and statistically significant.

Sit with that for a second, because it is the only figure in this story that answers the question people think they are arguing about.

Did the ban change anything measurable? Yes. About ten percentage points of account holding, which is roughly one in five of the children who had an account losing it. Modest, in the regulator's own word. Real, by its own statistics.

And it is missing from both arguments. The people who want the ban do not quote it because modest is not the word they are looking for. The people who oppose the ban do not quote it because it is not nothing.

I find that genuinely clarifying. When a number is inconvenient to everybody, it is usually the one worth knowing.

The same regulator's work also found the thing that should embarrass every platform in this story: around half the children who still had accounts said the platform had never checked their age, and 37 percent had simply entered an age of sixteen or over. The ban did not fail because children are cunning. It is leaking because nobody was checking.

The design flaw hiding inside the 85 percent

Go back to the detail everybody skips. Most of the children still using were on accounts they already had.

That is not children defeating a system. That is a system that was never pointed at them.

A ban can be built two ways. You can stop new accounts being created by people under the age, which is a gate on the way in. Or you can also require platforms to find and remove the under age accounts already on their books, which is a sweep of the people inside. The first is cheap, easy to announce and politically straightforward. The second is expensive, requires a platform to admit roughly how many under age users it has been carrying, and guarantees a wave of angry fourteen year olds and their parents.

If you gate the entrance and do not sweep the building, then on day one of your ban almost every child you were worried about is already inside, holding a working account, and your headline circumvention figure will be enormous within three months. Not because enforcement failed. Because enforcement was never asked to do that job.

Which is exactly what the regulator's other finding suggests was happening anyway: around half the children who still had accounts said the platform had never checked their age at all.

So the 85 percent is not really a measure of whether bans work. It is a measure of how this particular ban was built, and the answer to "did children get round it" is mostly that they did not have to.

This matters for Britain specifically, because our regulations have not been laid yet. The thing worth watching when they appear is not the headline age. It is whether they say anything about existing accounts, and who has to go looking for them. If they do not, you can write the three month story now.

How the same paper proves two opposite things

Here is the part I did not expect when I started looking into this.

Jonathan Haidt made the loudest case of the decade out of alarm. A generation rewired. An epidemic with a start date. A conclusion that keeps arriving ahead of the effect sizes that would carry it. I have written about that at length and I stand by it.

What I had not noticed is that the people who spend their days correcting him have started doing the same thing with the same material. A Psychology Today piece last month cited this BMJ paper as proof that the ban had failed.

The paper does not say the ban failed. It says we cannot tell yet. Its own authors say a decade.

So you now have two camps, pointing at one small three month study of one Australian state, each announcing that it settles a question the study explicitly declines to settle.

One side is frightened of the phones. The other is frightened of the ban. Both reach past what the study will carry, because a careful answer does not move anybody.

And I want to be honest about my own position in that, because I am not a neutral observer. I build a product that exists because I think a deadline is not a plan. That gives me a reason to want the ban to look insufficient. Knowing that is the only protection I have against it, and the reason I keep writing the regulator's inconvenient ten points down rather than quietly leaving them out.

The asymmetry that makes this worse

There is a structural reason the argument gets conducted this way, and it is worth naming because it will happen to Britain next.

A ban produces its bad news immediately and its good news slowly.

Circumvention is visible within weeks. A journalist can find a fourteen year old with an account in an afternoon. "They are all still on it" is available as a story almost at once, and it is true.

Whatever benefit a protected period might deliver, if it delivers one, shows up in mental health data years later, confounded by everything else that happened in those years, and will be contested when it arrives.

So the first two years of any ban will be dominated by evidence of failure, regardless of whether it works. Everyone who wants it to fail will have material. Everyone who wants it to succeed will have to say "wait", which is the losing move in public argument.

Britain's version lands in spring 2027, with the Culture Secretary having named March and no exact date officially confirmed. The regulations that would fix it were due before the end of this year and had not been laid when I wrote this.

You can therefore predict the next eighteen months of British commentary with some confidence. Three months after the checks start, somebody will find the teenagers who are still on it, and that will be reported as the ban failing. It will not be evidence of the ban failing. It will be evidence that bans leak, which we already know.

The test I now apply, and would ask you to apply

When somebody hands you a claim about the ban, three questions. They take about thirty seconds and they catch almost everything.

What did it measure, use or accounts? These are completely different things. Children still using a platform tells you about doors left open. Children holding an account tells you about enforcement. Time spent tells you about behaviour. Most coverage swaps them mid sentence.

Measured when, and for how long? Three months into a policy is a measure of implementation, not of effect. Anybody citing a three month figure as proof about children's mental health is telling you about themselves.

Does the finding point where the person quoting it is pointing? This is the one that catches the most. The BMJ paper is being cited by one camp for a conclusion its authors refuse. Go and read what the authors say they found. It is usually in the abstract, and it is usually more modest than the tweet.

What to do this week

This one is not about your child. It is about you, and it takes ten minutes.

Write down now what would change your mind about the ban.

Actually write it. On paper, or in a note on your phone, with today's date on it. Two sentences is plenty.

One sentence for each direction. What result, arriving in two or three years, would persuade you the ban was worth having? And what result would persuade you it was a distraction?
